title: Leaf River Streamflow Modeling — How This Project Works
text:
This site is the output of an experiment in which sixteen separate AI agents designed, built, calibrated and evaluated hydrological models for one watershed, coordinating only through files on disk.
The sections that follow explain the brief that started it, the vocabulary needed to read the rest of the site (agent, orchestration, skill, context, handoff), the guardrails that make the result trustworthy, and an honest account of what went wrong along the way. Read this first; the per-agent reports in the sidebar assume it.

title: Leaf River Streamflow Modeling — How This Project Works
section: 2.1 One thing in the brief could not be taken literally
text:
2.1 One thing in the brief could not be taken literally
The brief says the evaluation window is Oct 1 1948 – Sep 30 1951 and that “the previous period could be used as calibration”. There is no previous period: the data file begins on 1 October 1948, so the evaluation window sits at the very start of the record. Calibration therefore had to run forward from 1 October 1951 to the end of the record in 1988. This is logged in context/DECISIONS.md as a scaffold-time decision rather than silently assumed.
crumbs: Leaf River Streamflow Modeling — How This Project Works

title: Leaf River Streamflow Modeling — How This Project Works
text:
3.1 Agent
An agent is a language model given (a) a role, (b) a specific set of tools — read files, write files, run shell commands, search the web — and (c) a task, which it then carries out autonomously: deciding what to read, what code to write, what to check, and when it is finished.
The important property is that an agent is not a script. It makes judgement calls. Several of the most consequential results in this study came from an agent deciding to do something it was not explicitly told to do — and several of the problems came from the same freedom.
Each agent here is defined by a short Markdown file in .claude/agents/, e.g.:
---
name: a06-model-builder-2
description: Implements model slot 2 from config/models.yaml as a tested Python module.
tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep
model: opus
skills: [a06-model-builder-2]
---

title: Leaf River Streamflow Modeling — How This Project Works
text:
3.2 Sub-agent and context isolation
Each of the sixteen agents runs as a sub-agent: a separate conversation with its own fresh context window, launched by a coordinating “orchestrator” agent. This matters for a practical reason. A language model has a finite context; sixteen agents’ worth of exploration, dead ends and file dumps would not fit in one. Isolation means each agent sees only what it needs.
The cost of isolation is that agents cannot talk to each other. Everything they need to share must be written down — which is what the rest of this machinery is for.
crumbs: Leaf River Streamflow Modeling — How This Project Works

3.3 Orchestration and the dependency graph
Multi-agent orchestration is the coordination layer: deciding which agents run, in what order, what each one needs before it can start, and what it must produce before anything downstream may begin.
Here that graph lives in orchestration.yaml. It is a directed acyclic graph grouped into six phases; agents within a phase are independent and run in parallel.

title: Leaf River Streamflow Modeling — How This Project Works
text:
3.4 Skill
A skill is a detailed, reusable procedure attached to an agent — the difference between telling someone “do the data analysis” and handing them a laboratory protocol. Each agent here has one, in .claude/skills/<agent>/SKILL.md, typically 60–90 lines specifying the exact steps, the statistics to compute, the figures to produce, the checks that must pass, and the contents of its handoff.
Skills are what make an agent’s output predictable rather than merely plausible. They also encode institutional knowledge: a02’s skill, for example, mandates a Mann–Kendall trend test, a Pettitt change-point test and a double-mass curve — quality checks a general instruction would not have produced.

title: Leaf River Streamflow Modeling — How This Project Works
text:
3.5 Context, handoffs, and shared memory
Because agents cannot speak to one another, the project uses a set of append-only files as shared memory:







File
Purpose




context/CONTEXT.md
Each agent appends one section on finishing: key findings with units, outputs, what downstream agents must know.


context/handoffs/aNN.json
Machine-readable results: key_numbers, assumptions, downstream_notes addressed to specific later agents.


context/DECISIONS.md
Every non-obvious choice, with the alternatives considered and the reason.


context/ISSUES.md
Problems found in other agents’ work. Agents never edit each other’s files; they file an issue.


context/state.json
Which agents are pending / running / done. Gates the whole graph.


context/backups/ + git tags
Every agent commits and tags on finishing, so any step can be rolled back.



The downstream_notes field deserves emphasis: it lets an agent write a message addressed to a specific future agent that does not exist yet. a01 left a02 a note about unit conversion; a02 left the ML builders the exact scaling constants they were permitted to use.

title: Leaf River Streamflow Modeling — How This Project Works
section: 5.1 Things the agents caught that a script would not have
text:
5.1 Things the agents caught that a script would not have

a01 proved the data file’s identity. Asked only to characterize the watershed, it went further and matched the Q column against the USGS record for gauge 02472000: r = 1.000000 over 13,515 days. That turned an ambiguity about the calendar into a measurement.
a02 measured the units instead of assuming them. It found Q quantised at 0.0012544 mm/day — exactly 1 ft³/s over 1,950 km² — confirming both the units and the basin area independently.
a03 overrode its own instructions. Told to propose five models, it rejected HYMOD (a default choice) because HYMOD’s single linear store contradicts the non-linear recession a02 had measured, and substituted HBV-light with an argument.
a08 chose provable correctness over fidelity. Implementing SAC-SMA, it dropped a line from the original Fortran that destroys mass, because keeping it would have made the conservation invariants unprovable. It logged the deviation rather than hiding it.
crumbs: Leaf River Streamflow Modeling — How This Project Works

title: Leaf River Streamflow Modeling — How This Project Works
text:
5.2 Things that went wrong

The evaluation window was initially wrong. An early translation of the brief’s calendar dates into row indices produced rows 265:1360 instead of 0:1095. Both windows contain exactly 1,003 metric days, which is why the error was not obvious. It was caught by cross-checking against the user’s earlier study and confirmed independently by PET seasonality and the USGS match (ISSUE-001).
Agents collided on shared files. Running five builders concurrently exposed that backup.sh and state.py were not safe under parallel use — concurrent git commits fight over index.lock, and a read-modify-write on state.json loses siblings’ updates. Both were made atomic. Two agents also filed different issues under the same number, which had to be renumbered.
A declared compute budget was never enforced. config/optimization.yaml specified a 90-minute cap for the LSTM search, but the runner never read that block: study.optimize() was called with no timeout=. The search ran over seven hours and produced nothing (ISSUE-006). It was replaced by a budgeted alternative agent that enforces its deadline in code, which finished the same experiment in 7.6 minutes. The lesson is general: a limit that lives only in a configuration file is not a limit.

title: Leaf River Streamflow Modeling — How This Project Works
section: 5.3 The headline result contradicted the design
text:
5.3 The headline result contradicted the design
The study was built around a complexity gradient — regression → GR4J → HBV → SAC-SMA → LSTM — to measure how much complexity buys. On the held-out window the answer was nothing: the 26-coefficient ridge regression achieved the highest NSE of any candidate, and the rank correlation between number of fitted quantities and KGE across the five models was −0.70.
Because the hypothesis was pre-registered, that is reported as a falsification rather than quietly reframed. The H1-risk section of the model report was written after the models were built but before the held-out window was opened, specifically so the inconvenient evidence could not be presented as though it had been expected all along.

4.4 Surrogate / Bayesian








Algorithm
Principle
When it pays




EGO / GP-EI (Jones et al. 1998)
Gaussian-process surrogate, expected-improvement sampling
expensive evaluations (> 1 s) — not our slots 2–4


TPE (Bergstra et al. 2011)
density-ratio model \(p(x\mid y<y^\ast)/p(x\mid y\ge y^\ast)\)
mixed integer/continuous, 25–1,000 expensive trials → slots 1 and 5


DYCORS / RBF (Regis and Shoemaker 2013)
radial-basis surrogate + dynamic coordinate perturbation
high-dimensional expensive problems



Implementation: optuna 5.0.0 (Akiba et al. 2019) with MedianPruner (prune a trial whose intermediate validation score is below the running median — the single most effective way to buy trials for slot 5).

title: Optimization algorithms, settings and budgets for the five Leaf River model slots
section: 4.5 Uncertainty-aware sampling (not used for the ranking, but available)
text:
4.5 Uncertainty-aware sampling (not used for the ranking, but available)
GLUE (Beven and Binley 1992), DREAM\(_{(ZS)}\) (Vrugt 2016), SCEM-UA (Vrugt, Gupta, Bouten, et al. 2003), MCMC with emcee (Foreman-Mackey et al. 2013), ROPE, and Sobol’/Morris screening with SALib (Herman and Usher 2017). These answer “how well determined is the parameter set?”, not “what is the best parameter set?”. The project ranks deterministic single-parameter-set models by KGE and NSE (CLAUDE.md), so they stay out of the calibration path; a13/a14 may run a cheap Sobol’ screening as a diagnostic of which parameters the objective can actually identify.
crumbs: Optimization algorithms, settings and budgets for the five Leaf River model slots

title: Optimization algorithms, settings and budgets for the five Leaf River model slots
text:
4.6 Multi-objective
NSGA-II/III (Deb et al. 2002) via pymoo (Blank and Deb 2020), MOSCEM (Vrugt, Gupta, Bastidas, et al. 2003) and Borg produce a Pareto front in (KGE, NSE) space. Agent 4 measured that KGE and NSE are only rank-correlated at ≈ 0.70 on this record, so a front would be genuinely two-dimensional — but the study’s final ranking is single-objective by construction, and a front cannot be handed to a16 as one parameter set. The 50/50 scalarisation is the project’s declared compromise. Rejected for the calibration path, recommended only as an optional diagnostic for slot 4.

def evals_to(model, algo, seed, target):
    c = CURVES.get(f"{model}|{algo}|{seed}")
    if c is None: return np.nan
    hit = np.nonzero((1 - c) >= target)[0]
    return float(hit[0] + 1) if hit.size else np.nan

Figure 2: Experiment A. Left: final objective of each seed (points) around the algorithm median; the grey band is +/- 1e-4, the practical convergence tolerance. Right: equifinality — the across-seed coefficient of variation of each best parameter value for HBV-light, per algorithm.





Reading of Experiment A.

On GR4J (4 parameters) the problem is, in practice, solved: SCE-UA, DE, CMA-ES, dual annealing and multi-start Nelder–Mead all land on the same optimum to better than \(10^{-6}\) objective units, with zero spread across seeds. CMA-ES gets there in ≈ 900 evaluations, SCE-UA in ≈ 3,500, DE in ≈ 5,000. Only PSO (default inertia/cognitive settings) misses, by ≈ 0.002 with a seed spread of 0.002 — i.e. PSO is the one algorithm whose tuning would itself need tuning.
On HBV-light (9 parameters, threshold outlet) the ranking separates: CMA-ES reaches the best value with a seed spread of \(9\times10^{-6}\), followed by dual annealing, DE, SCE-UA and multi-start Nelder–Mead; DDS and PSO fall short by 0.8–2.2 \(\times10^{-3}\). All differences are, hydrologically, nothing — the worst algorithm is 0.002 objective units behind the best, while a04 measured 0.02–0.06 units of regret between objective functions and 0.05–0.08 between calibration periods. Algorithm choice is a second-order effect; convergence bookkeeping is not.
The right-hand panel shows the real story: parameter values scatter across seeds far more than the objective does (equifinality). For the algorithms with the largest objective spread (DDS, PSO) the parameter CV reaches 0.3–0.6 — the same objective is reached from very different parameter sets. This is why a11–a15 must report the across-seed parameter spread, not only the best set.
Transfer to the internal-validation window is flat across algorithms (column O validation): a better calibration objective did not buy a better out-of-sample objective beyond the third decimal. Squeezing the last \(10^{-4}\) out of the search is not where the score comes from.

title: Optimization algorithms, settings and budgets for the five Leaf River model slots
text:
7.1 Slot 1 — arx_api_ridge (7 hyperparameters + 21 closed-form coefficients)

Algorithm: Optuna TPE (Bergstra et al. 2011; Akiba et al. 2019), 256 Sobol’ start-up trials + 744 TPE trials, multivariate=True, × 5 seeds (42–46); cross-check with DE (3,000 evaluations) and the pure Sobol’ sample as a noise reference. TPE is chosen because the outer problem is mixed: six continuous hyperparameters plus the integer n_lag, over which the objective is piecewise constant — exactly the structure a density-ratio sampler handles and a Gaussian assumption does not.
Inner estimator: the ridge solve is closed form (Hoerl and Kennard 1970), so each trial costs one fit (measured 25 ms) — 1,000 trials × 5 seeds ≈ 2 min.
Windows: coefficients on internal train, hyperparameters selected on internal validation (a03/a04), then a closed-form refit on the full calibration metric window with the selected hyperparameters. The refitted object is the artefact that goes to a16.
Parsimony rule (over-fitting guard, 7 hyperparameters selected on 2,557 days): among all configurations within 0.002 objective units of the best validation score, take the one with the smallest n_lag and the largest log10_ridge_alpha. Report train and validation objective; a gap larger than 0.03 is a flag.
Transforms: lam_slow and lam_pet are sampled uniformly in \(\log(1-\lambda)\) (i.e. uniform in log memory \(1/(1-\lambda)\)). Their bounds 0.95–0.999 and 0.80–0.999 correspond to memories of 20–1,000 d and 5–1,000 d; a uniform-in-\(\lambda\) sample would put half of its points in the 20–40 d band and explore the intended decade-wide range with a handful of trials.
crumbs: Optimization algorithms, settings and budgets for the five Leaf River model slots

title: Optimization algorithms, settings and budgets for the five Leaf River model slots
text:
7.2 Slot 2 — gr4j (4 parameters)

Algorithm: SCE-UA, ngs = 2n+1 = 9, kstop = 10, pcento = 1e-4, peps = 1e-6, budget cap 30,000, 10 seeds (42–51); cross-check CMA-ES and DE with the same cap; finally a 2,000-evaluation Nelder–Mead polish from the overall best point.
Why SCE-UA and not the (slightly faster) CMA-ES? On this slot every global method finds the same optimum (Exp. A), so speed is irrelevant — 10 SCE-UA seeds cost ≈ 45 s. SCE-UA was developed by Duan et al. (1992) on the Leaf River daily record and is the method every reader of this basin’s literature expects; using it here and cross-checking with two structurally different algorithms is the more defensible choice. The cross-check is what actually certifies convergence.
Expected outcome: seed spread \(< 10^{-6}\), ≈ 100,000 evaluations in total, ≈ 7 min wall time.
crumbs: Optimization algorithms, settings and budgets for the five Leaf River model slots

title: Optimization algorithms, settings and budgets for the five Leaf River model slots
text:
7.3 Slot 3 — hbv_light (9 parameters, non-smooth)

Algorithm: CMA-ES, sigma0 = 0.25 on the unit cube, default population \(4+\lfloor 3\ln d\rfloor\), tolfun = 1e-10, cap 50,000, 10 seeds; cross-check SCE-UA (ngs = 19) and DE; Nelder–Mead polish.
Why CMA-ES? It won Experiment A on this exact structure — best median objective, the smallest seed spread (\(9\times10^{-6}\)) and the fewest evaluations (≈ 4,500 median). Its covariance adaptation is what handles the strong K1–PERC–UZL interaction; the unit-cube mapping is what makes a single step size legitimate across parameters spanning 0.0005–1,000 in raw units.
Forbidden: L-BFGS-B and any finite-difference gradient (Exp. E: 0 of 15 single starts succeeded on this surface; Kavetski and Kuczera (2007)). Transforms: linear — Exp. C shows the log map buys nothing here.
Watch: a bound-active K1 or K2 at the optimum is a message about the bounds in config/models.yaml, to be reported as an ISSUE, not silently widened.
crumbs: Optimization algorithms, settings and budgets for the five Leaf River model slots

title: Optimization algorithms, settings and budgets for the five Leaf River model slots
section: 7.4 Slot 4 — sacsma (15 parameters, non-smooth, integer sub-stepping)
text:
7.4 Slot 4 — sacsma (15 parameters, non-smooth, integer sub-stepping)

Algorithm: SCE-UA with ngs = 15, cap 100,000 per seed, 10 seeds; cross-check CMA-ES (10 seeds, cap 60,000) and DDS (5 seeds, cap 60,000).
Why this budget? Experiment D inflates the same threshold surface from 9 to 15 search dimensions: the evaluation count needed by CMA-ES and SCE-UA grows by roughly a factor 3, and no algorithm needed more than ≈ 30,000 evaluations to stop improving. A 100,000 cap is therefore ≈ 3× the measured requirement, and it still costs only ≈ 8 min per seed at 5 ms/evaluation. Duan et al. (1994) recommend ngs of the order of \(n\) for problems of this size, and Sorooshian et al. (1993) calibrated SAC-SMA on this record with SCE-UA. Experiment B confirms that the result is insensitive to ngs (5, 10, 19 and 20 complexes agree to \(5\times10^{-5}\) on the 9-parameter surface; fewer complexes simply stop earlier).
Honest caveat: in Experiment D it is CMA-ES, not SCE-UA, that reaches the best 15-dimensional value (0.919568 in ≈ 7,100 evaluations versus 0.919311 for SCE-UA). SCE-UA is kept as the declared primary for continuity with this basin’s literature, but the two are treated as equal partners: step 7 of the protocol selects the best set over all seeds and all cross-check algorithms.
DDS in the portfolio because it is the method designed for a fixed, comparatively small budget (Tolson and Shoemaker 2007) and it degrades most gracefully in dimension; it is the safety net if the real SAC-SMA turns out to be 4× more expensive than estimated.
Diagnostics: report the KGE decomposition at the optimum, the across-seed spread of every parameter (LZPK/LZFPM equifinality is expected), and the warm-up sensitivity check described in config/optimization.yaml (a03 asks for 730 warm-up days; only 366 exist inside the calibration window and only 92 before the evaluation metric window — see Section 14).
crumbs: Optimization algorithms, settings and budgets for the five Leaf River model slots

title: Optimization algorithms, settings and budgets for the five Leaf River model slots
text:
7.5 Slot 5 — lstm_seq2seq (10 hyperparameters + ≈ 20,500 weights)

Inner: AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter 2019) with gradient-norm clipping at 1.0, the per-window NSE* loss of Kratzert et al. (2019) with the first warmup_steps masked, learning-rate halving at epochs 60/120, early stopping with patience 20 on the composite objective of the full internal-validation simulation (Prechelt 1998) — never a per-minibatch efficiency (config/metrics.yaml).
Outer: Optuna TPE with MedianPruner(n_startup_trials=5, n_warmup_steps=15, interval_steps=5), 25 trials (the a03 cap), ≤ 60 epochs per trial, and a hard 90 min study timeout.
Final: 5 members with seeds 42–46, ≤ 200 epochs each, per-member wall cap 20 min; the slot-5 prediction is their arithmetic mean (a03). No refit on the full calibration window — the validation window is the only over-fitting guard (a03 decision).
Budget arithmetic (Table 9): the default architecture costs ≈ 1.8 s/epoch, so 200 epochs take 6 min; the largest admissible architecture (hidden 128, 2 layers) costs 5.9 s/epoch → 20 min. Worst case 90 min (HP stage, capped) + 5 × 20 min (members) = 3.2 h, which is why the per-member cap and the study timeout are mandatory, not advisory. Expected case ≈ 1.5 h.
If MPS results are not bit-reproducible between runs, fall back to CPU and record the deviation.

2.1 Squared-error family
\[
\mathrm{MSE}=\frac1n\sum (s_i-o_i)^2,\qquad \mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}},\qquad
\mathrm{NSE}=1-\frac{\sum (s_i-o_i)^2}{\sum (o_i-\mu_o)^2}
\]
\[
\mathrm{NSE}_{T}=1-\frac{\sum (T(s_i)-T(o_i))^2}{\sum (T(o_i)-\mu_{T(o)})^2},\quad
T\in\{\sqrt{\cdot},\ \log,\ 1/\cdot,\ \text{Box–Cox}_\lambda\},\qquad
\mathrm{NNSE}=\frac{1}{2-\mathrm{NSE}}
\]
Gupta et al. (2009) decomposition, used throughout this report: \[
\mathrm{NSE}=2\alpha r-\alpha^2-\beta_n^2,\qquad
\alpha=\frac{\sigma_s}{\sigma_o},\quad \beta_n=\frac{\mu_s-\mu_o}{\sigma_o}.
\]

NoteInformation-theoretic and probabilistic scores



Mutual information \(I(s;o)\), CRPS and Wasserstein distances were considered. CRPS requires a predictive distribution; all five model slots are deterministic and the final ranking is deterministic, so CRPS is only meaningful if an ensemble is submitted — it is therefore not part of the objective and not part of the report. The 1-Wasserstein distance between FDCs is implemented (FDC_W1_log) because it is a pure distribution-shape diagnostic: a model can have \(W_1=0\) and \(r=0\), which makes it a clean complement to KGE’s \(r\) term. Mutual information was rejected as an objective: on 13 149 daily values it needs binning/KDE choices that are themselves tuning parameters, and it is invariant to any monotone transform — including a 50 % volume bias.

title: Performance metrics for daily streamflow and the calibration objective for Leaf River
text:
6.1 Design

Surrogate 1 — HyMOD (5 parameters: \(C_{max}\), \(b_{exp}\), \(\alpha\), \(R_s\), \(R_q\)): a PDM storage (Moore 1985) feeding one slow and three quick linear reservoirs. HyMOD is the classic Leaf River model (Boyle et al. 2000; Vrugt et al. 2003), which makes it the most defensible surrogate available.
Surrogate 2 — NLRes (5 parameters: \(S_{max}\), \(\beta\), \(d\), \(k_f\), \(k_s\)): HBV-style power-law saturation runoff, a linear fast reservoir and a non-linear slow reservoir \(q=k_sS^{1.5}\), chosen because a02 found a non-linear recession (Brutsaert–Nieber \(b=1.68\)). Two structurally different surrogates guard against a conclusion that is an artefact of one model.
Optimiser: SciPy differential_evolution, seed 42, popsize 15, maxiter 150, tol \(10^{-8}\), polish — identical budget for every objective, so differences are attributable to the objective.
Splits (all inside calibration):



Code
from numba import njit, prange

@njit(cache=True, fastmath=True)
def _hymod(P, E, cmax, bexp, alpha, Rs, Rq):
    n = P.shape[0]; Q = np.empty(n)
    x_loss = 0.0; x_slow = 2.3503 / (Rs * 22.5); x_q1 = x_q2 = x_q3 = 0.0
    b1 = bexp + 1.0; cm_b = cmax / b1
    for t in range(n):
        Pval = P[t]; PETval = E[t]; xn_prev = x_loss
        arg = 1.0 - b1 * xn_prev / cmax
        if arg < 0.0: arg = 0.0
        ct_prev = cmax * (1.0 - arg ** (1.0 / b1))
        UT1 = Pval - cmax + ct_prev
        if UT1 < 0.0: UT1 = 0.0
        Pval = Pval - UT1
        dummy = (ct_prev + Pval) / cmax
        if dummy > 1.0: dummy = 1.0
        xn = cm_b * (1.0 - (1.0 - dummy) ** b1)
        UT2 = Pval - (xn - xn_prev)
        if UT2 < 0.0: UT2 = 0.0
        evap = (1.0 - (cm_b - xn) / cm_b) * PETval
        if evap > xn: evap = xn
        x_loss = xn - evap
        UQ = alpha * (UT1 + UT2); US = (1.0 - alpha) * (UT1 + UT2)
        x_slow = (1.0 - Rs) * x_slow + (1.0 - Rs) * US; QS = (Rs / (1.0 - Rs)) * x_slow
        x_q1 = (1.0 - Rq) * x_q1 + (1.0 - Rq) * UQ;  o1 = (Rq / (1.0 - Rq)) * x_q1
        x_q2 = (1.0 - Rq) * x_q2 + (1.0 - Rq) * o1;  o2 = (Rq / (1.0 - Rq)) * x_q2
        x_q3 = (1.0 - Rq) * x_q3 + (1.0 - Rq) * o2;  o3 = (Rq / (1.0 - Rq)) * x_q3
        q = QS + o3
        Q[t] = q if q > 1e-9 else 1e-9
    return Q

@njit(cache=True, fastmath=True)
def _nlres(P, E, Smax, beta, d, kf, ks):
    n = P.shape[0]; Q = np.empty(n)
    S = 0.5 * Smax; Sf = 0.0; Ss = 10.0
    for t in range(n):
        p = P[t]; ratio = S / Smax
        if ratio > 1.0: ratio = 1.0
        r = p * ratio ** beta
        S = S + p - r
        ea = E[t] * (S / Smax)
        if ea > S: ea = S
        S = S - ea
        if S > Smax:
            r += S - Smax; S = Smax
        Sf = Sf + d * r; qf = kf * Sf; Sf = Sf - qf
        Ss = Ss + (1.0 - d) * r; qs = ks * Ss ** 1.5
        if qs > Ss: qs = Ss
        Ss = Ss - qs
        q = qf + qs
        Q[t] = q if q > 1e-9 else 1e-9
    return Q

@njit(parallel=True, cache=True)
def simulate_batch(P, E, theta, which):
    ns = theta.shape[0]; nt = P.shape[0]; out = np.empty((ns, nt))
    for i in prange(ns):
        if which == 0:
            out[i] = _hymod(P, E, theta[i, 0], theta[i, 1], theta[i, 2], theta[i, 3], theta[i, 4])
        else:
            out[i] = _nlres(P, E, theta[i, 0], theta[i, 1], theta[i, 2], theta[i, 3], theta[i, 4])
    return out

BOUNDS = {0: np.array([[1.0, 500.0], [0.1, 2.0], [0.10, 0.99], [0.0005, 0.15], [0.10, 0.95]]),
          1: np.array([[50.0, 800.0], [0.5, 6.0], [0.05, 0.95], [0.05, 0.90], [0.001, 0.20]])}
PNAMES = {0: ["cmax", "bexp", "alpha", "Rs", "Rq"], 1: ["Smax", "beta", "d", "kf", "ks"]}

CANDIDATES = {
    "NSE": mx.nse, "KGE": kge, "KGE_2012": mx.kge_2012, "KGE_2021": mx.kge_2021,
    "KGE_np": mx.kge_np, "NSE_sqrt": mx.nse_sqrt, "NSE_log": mx.nse_log, "NSE_inv": mx.nse_inv,
    "NSE_bc025": lambda s, o: mx.nse_boxcox(s, o, lam=0.25),
    "KGE_sqrt": mx.kge_sqrt, "KGE_log": mx.kge_log,
    "KGEmix_sqrt50": lambda s, o: mx.kge_mix(s, o, w=0.50, transform="sqrt"),
    "KGEmix_sqrt75": lambda s, o: mx.kge_mix(s, o, w=0.75, transform="sqrt"),
    "KGEmix_log50":  lambda s, o: mx.kge_mix(s, o, w=0.50, transform="log"),
    "NSEmix_log50":  lambda s, o: mx.nse_mix(s, o, w=0.50, transform="log"),
    "KGE_NSE_50":    lambda s, o: mx.kge_nse_mix(s, o, w=0.50),
    "negMAE": lambda s, o: -mx.mae(s, o), "DE": mx.de_metric,
    # three post-hoc variants used to check whether a transformed third term adds anything
    "KNS_333": lambda s, o: (kge(s, o) + mx.nse(s, o) + mx.kge_sqrt(s, o)) / 3.0,
    "KNS_442": lambda s, o: 0.4 * kge(s, o) + 0.4 * mx.nse(s, o) + 0.2 * mx.kge_sqrt(s, o),
    "KN_7030": lambda s, o: 0.7 * kge(s, o) + 0.3 * mx.nse(s, o),
    "negFDC_W1": lambda s, o: -mx.fdc_wasserstein(s, o),
    "LL_bc025": lambda s, o: mx.loglik_boxcox(s, o, lam=0.25) / 1e4,
    "Willmott_d": mx.willmott_d,
}
# objectives carried through ALL four splits (the expensive part); the remaining candidates are
# screened on the temporal split only. KGE_np and NSE_log are screened only (KGE_np costs ~4x).
CORE = ["NSE", "KGE", "KGE_2012", "NSE_sqrt", "KGE_sqrt", "KGE_log",

The evaluation window has mean-\(Q\) ratio 1.29 relative to calibration and a maximum (45.9 mm/d) below the calibration maximum (64.0). The three “wet” splits reproduce exactly that situation inside calibration — ratio 1.20–1.46, test maximum always below the training maximum — so a model must extrapolate in wetness but not in magnitude. The temporal split is the useful mirror image (test 6 % drier than train): an objective that is robust must survive both directions.

from scipy.optimize import differential_evolution

def optimise(mask, which, fobj, seed=SEED, maxiter=150, popsize=15):
    b = BOUNDS[which]; o = OBS[mask]
    def cost(th):
        s = simulate_batch(P, PET, np.atleast_2d(th), which)[0]
        v = fobj(s[mask], o)
        return -v if np.isfinite(v) else 1e6
    res = differential_evolution(cost, list(map(tuple, b)), seed=seed, maxiter=maxiter,
                                 popsize=popsize, tol=1e-8, mutation=(0.3, 1.0),
                                 recombination=0.9, polish=True, init="sobol", workers=1)
    return res.x, -res.fun

t0 = time.time(); rows = []
for which, mname in ((0, "HyMOD"), (1, "NLRes")):
    for sname, (mtr, mte) in SPLITS.items():
        names = list(CANDIDATES) if sname.startswith("temporal") else CORE
        for cname in names:
            th, val = optimise(mtr, which, CANDIDATES[cname])
            s = simulate_batch(P, PET, np.atleast_2d(th), which)[0]
            rows.append(dict(model=mname, split=sname, objective=cname, obj_train=val,
                             KGE_train=kge(s[mtr], OBS[mtr]), NSE_train=nse(s[mtr], OBS[mtr]),

title: Performance metrics for daily streamflow and the calibration objective for Leaf River
text:
7.1 The decision
Calibrate on \(\mathcal{O}=0.5\,\mathrm{KGE}(Q)+0.5\,\mathrm{NSE}(Q)\) — maximise — on 1952-10-01…1988-09-30; equivalently minimise \(1-\mathcal{O}\).
This is not the answer the catalogue alone would have suggested (a KGE + \(\sqrt{Q}\) composite); it is what Section 6 produced. The decisive numbers:







Criterion
Evidence




Alignment with the reported metrics
The objective is the unweighted average of the two reported metrics on untransformed \(Q\) — nothing is optimised that is not reported, and nothing reported is left out. No transform, no \(\varepsilon\), no tuning constant other than the 50/50 weight.


The two terms are not redundant
Over 6 000 behavioural HyMOD simulations the Spearman rank correlation between KGE and NSE is only ≈0.7 (Figure 6): KGE and NSE genuinely disagree about which parameter set is better on this record, so averaging them is a real multi-criteria compromise, not a re-scaling.


Robustness to the skew and to volume bias
KGE’s \(\beta\) term supplies the water-balance control that NSE lacks at CV = 2.107 (factor 14–89, Table 7), while NSE’s stronger timing sensitivity (Section 5 item 2) compensates KGE’s weaker one. The pair covers each other’s blind spots.


Transfer to a wetter period
Table 12: worst-case regret 0.056 (KGE) and 0.047 (NSE) — the only candidate of the 24 that keeps both below 0.06. KGE-only calibration has a worst case of 0.162 in NSE, NSE-only 0.107 in KGE. On the wet blocks the recommendation reaches mean KGE 0.773 / NSE 0.725 against 0.783/0.697 (KGE-only) and 0.743/0.734 (NSE-only): it gives up ≈0.010 KGE to gain ≈0.028 NSE.


Parsimony
Three further variants were run through all 8 experiments: \((\mathrm{KGE}+\mathrm{NSE}+\mathrm{KGE}(\sqrt Q))/3\), \(0.4/0.4/0.2\) and \(0.7\,\mathrm{KGE}+0.3\,\mathrm{NSE}\). The first two are indistinguishable from the recommendation (all out-of-sample means differ by < 0.001); the 70/30 weighting trades 0.004 KGE for 0.008 NSE and doubles the worst case. The simplest member of the tied group wins.


Optimiser and ML compatibility
Smooth, bounded above by 1, ~0.9 ms per evaluation on 13 149 days, and differentiable everywhere — a10’s global searches, a11–a15’s calibrations and a09’s gradient training all use the same scalar.









NoteHonest limitation



The recommendation does not improve low flows: out-of-sample log-NSE on the wet blocks is 0.666 for the recommendation against 0.761 for sqrt-NSE and 0.591 for KGE-only, and the high-flow bias FHV is −16.9 % against −12.3 % for KGE-only. Balancing the hydrograph and maximising the two reported metrics are different goals, and config/project.yaml asks for the second. The low-flow and high-flow behaviour is therefore controlled through the acceptance checks in config/metrics.yaml (|PBIAS| ≤ 10 %, \(\beta\in[0.90,1.10]\), \(\alpha\in[0.85,1.15]\), \(|\mathrm{FHV}| \le 25\) %, \(|\Delta\mathrm{BFI}|\le0.15\)), which a11–a15 must report, not through the objective. A slot that passes the acceptance checks and maximises \(\mathcal{O}\) is both hydrologically sound and competitive in the ranking.

title: Performance metrics for daily streamflow and the calibration objective for Leaf River
text:
7.2 Why not each alternative

Plain KGE (2009). The ranking metric, and the declared fallback. It gives the best out-of-sample KGE (regret 0.020 vs 0.026) — but the worst NSE of the whole KGE family (regret 0.047, worst case 0.162, wet-block NSE 0.697). Since NSE is reported too, paying 0.006 KGE to remove that exposure is the better bet.
NSE. Nearly blind to volume bias at CV = 2.107 (Table 7): a 10 % volume error costs 0.0023 NSE and 0.100 KGE. NSE-only calibrations produced the largest \(|\beta-1|\) on every wet test block (mean \(\beta\) = 1.103 vs 1.089) and the largest KGE regret (0.052). Never alone.
RMSE / MSE / Gaussian likelihood. Monotone transformations of each other and of NSE for a fixed observation window — identical argmax, identical weakness. Not separate options. (LL_bc025 and NSE_bc025 returned bit-identical parameter sets in Table 10, which is the empirical demonstration of that equivalence.)
KGE′ (2012). \(\gamma=\mathrm{CV}_s/\mathrm{CV}_o\) cancels a pure scaling error, so a uniformly biased model is penalised once instead of twice. It wins single wet blocks (KGE 0.909 on WY1961–63) but has the worst NSE regret of the KGE family (0.118) and out-of-sample log-NSE 0.11: it buys KGE by wrecking the low-flow end.
KGE″ (2021). Built for \(\mu_o\to0\) (ephemeral rivers). At CV = 2.107 it divides the bias by 2.1 before squaring and degenerates towards NSE; on the temporal split it was strictly worse than KGE for both surrogates. Leaf River is perennial — there is nothing to fix.
Non-parametric KGE. Robust and FDC-based, and the best objective for HyMOD on the temporal split, but it collapsed for the second surrogate (test NSE 0.257) because it optimises ranks and FDC shape rather than event magnitudes. Mean KGE regret 0.077. Retained as a diagnostic.
log-NSE / log-KGE / inverse-NSE. Section 5 items 3–4: they cannot see a 30 % raw-variance error and they explode on 0.3 mm/d of low-flow noise. In the transfer experiment KGE_log was the worst objective tested (mean KGE regret 0.181, NSE regret 0.579; test NSE −0.47 for one surrogate) and inverse-NSE was second worst. With only 92 warm-up days before the evaluation metric window, an objective dominated by the slowest store is also the most exposed to initial-state error.
MAE. A genuinely strong performer (best mean test KGE on the temporal split) and robust to the tail, but it is not one of the reported metrics, it has no diagnostic decomposition, and its worst-case KGE regret (0.091) is 1.6× the recommendation’s.
Formal likelihoods (GL, AR(1)). Only justified if a10 chooses DREAM and the deliverable were predictive uncertainty. They add 3–5 nuisance parameters and, in the Gaussian case, reduce to NSE.
Signature / Pareto multi-objective. A Pareto front cannot be handed to a11–a15 as a single number and the final ranking is single-objective by construction. Signatures are used as acceptance checks instead (Section 8).

6.1 Verification of the record start date and period definition
ISSUE-001 (evaluation window given as row indices 265:1360 vs. as the calendar window 1948-10-01…1951-09-30) was resolved by the user on 2026-09-15: config/project.yaml now uses periods.definition: dates. This subsection verifies that resolution from the data themselves.

n = len(d); t = np.arange(n)
def harmonic(y, T=365.25):
    X = np.c_[np.ones(n), np.cos(2*np.pi*t/T), np.sin(2*np.pi*t/T)]
    b = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
    amp  = float(np.hypot(b[1], b[2]))
    tpk  = float((np.arctan2(b[2], b[1])/(2*np.pi)) % 1.0 * T)     # days after row 0
    r2   = float(1 - ((y - X@b)**2).sum()/((y - y.mean())**2).sum())
    return b[0], amp, tpk, r2

H = {}
for v, y in [("P", Pv), ("PET", PETv), ("Q", Qv)]:
    H[v] = harmonic(y)

PET phase — the fitted annual harmonic (R² = 0.46) peaks 278 days after row 0. 8.1 Baseflow separation (Lyne and Hollick 1979; Eckhardt 2005)


Code
def lyne_hollick(q, a=0.925, passes=3):
    b = q.copy()
    for p in range(passes):
        y = b[::-1] if p % 2 else b
        f = np.zeros_like(y); f[0] = y[0]
        for i in range(1, len(y)):
            f[i] = a*f[i-1] + (1+a)/2*(y[i]-y[i-1])
        bf = np.minimum(y, y - np.maximum(f, 0))
        b = bf[::-1] if p % 2 else bf
    return np.clip(b, 0, q)

bf = lyne_hollick(Qv); qf = Qv - bf

rec_mask = np.r_[False, np.diff(Qv) < 0] & (Pv < 0.1)
runs, c = [], 0
for i, m in enumerate(rec_mask):

for a_, b_ in runs:
    seg = Qv[a_-1:b_]

    Qm.append((seg[:-1]+seg[1:])/2); dQm.append(-np.diff(seg))
ks = np.array(ks); Qm = np.concatenate(Qm); dQm = np.concatenate(dQm)
ok = dQm > 0
bBN, aBN = np.polyfit(np.log(Qm[ok]), np.log(dQm[ok]), 1)

axs[1].hist(ks, bins=40, color="#2ca02c")

fig.tight_layout(); save(fig, "recession"); plt.show()

      f"{100*sum(b_-a_ for a_,b_ in runs)/len(d):.1f}% of the record)")
print(f"master recession constant k = {k_med:.4f} /d  ->  residence time tau = {tau:.1f} d")
print(f"Brutsaert-Nieber exponent b = {bBN:.2f} (b=1 linear reservoir, b~1.5 Boussinesq) , a = {np.exp(aBN):.3f}")
def eckhardt(q, a, BFImax):
    b = np.empty_like(q); b[0] = q[0]*BFImax
    for i in range(1, len(q)):
        b[i] = min(((1-BFImax)*a*b[i-1] + (1-a)*BFImax*q[i])/(1-a*BFImax), q[i])
    return b
BFI_E = {bm: float(eckhardt(Qv, k_med, bm).sum()/Qv.sum()) for bm in (0.50, 0.80)}

The Brutsaert–Nieber exponent b = 1.68 is clearly non-linear (> 1): recession is faster at high flow, which a single linear reservoir cannot reproduce — two parallel stores (or a non-linear store) are needed.

Setup (paths, style, helpers)
import json, os, tempfile, urllib.request, warnings
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib as mpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
ROOT = Path.cwd().parents[0] if Path.cwd().name == "reports" else Path.cwd()
FIG  = ROOT / "results" / "figures"
FIG.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
CACHE = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "lr_a01_cache"
CACHE.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

np.random.seed(42)
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "savefig.dpi": 150, "font.size": 9,
                     "axes.grid": True, "grid.alpha": 0.3, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False})

def fetch(url: str, name: str, timeout: int = 120) -> Path | None:
    """Download `url` once into a temp cache. Returns None if the network is unavailable."""
    p = CACHE / name
    if p.exists() and p.stat().st_size > 0:
        return p
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=timeout) as r:
            p.write_bytes(r.read())
        return p if p.stat().st_size > 0 else None
    except Exception as e:                                   # pragma: no cover
        print(f"[warn] could not fetch {name}: {e}")
        return None

def rdb(path: Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read a USGS RDB file (comment lines '#', second row = format codes)."""
    import io
    txt = "".join(l for l in open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") if not l.startswith("#"))
    return pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(txt), sep="\t", dtype=str).iloc[1:].reset_index(drop=True)

import sys
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))
from src.common.data import load_data, slice_run, metric_mask
import io

df  = load_data()
cal = slice_run(df, "calibration")          # 1951-10-01 .. 1988-09-30 (no evaluation rows)
cm  = cal[metric_mask(cal, "calibration")]  # 1952-10-01 .. 1988-09-30

dv_p = fetch("https://waterservices.usgs.gov/nwis/dv/?format=rdb&sites=02472000"
             "&startDT=1951-10-01&endDT=1988-09-30&parameterCd=00060&statCd=00003",
             "dv_cal.rdb", timeout=300)
res = []
if dv_p:
    u = rdb(dv_p)
    col = [c for c in u.columns if c.endswith("_00060_00003") and not c.endswith("_cd")][0]
    u["date"] = pd.to_datetime(u["datetime"])
    usgs = u.set_index("date")[col].astype(float) * 0.0283168      # ft³/s → m³/s
    common = cal.index.intersection(usgs.index)
    fq, uq = cal["Q"].loc[common].to_numpy(), usgs.loc[common].to_numpy()
    A_ls = 86.4 * np.sum(uq * fq) / np.sum(fq * fq)
    for A in (1924.4, 1944.0, A_ls, 1950.0):
        conv = uq * 86.4 / A
        res.append((f"{A:,.1f}", f"{np.corrcoef(fq, conv)[0,1]:.6f}",
                    f"{(fq.mean()-conv.mean())/conv.mean()*100:+.2f} %",
                    f"{np.sqrt(((fq-conv)**2).mean()):.4f}"))
    lags = {k: np.corrcoef(fq[2:-2], (uq*86.4/A_ls)[2+k:len(uq)-2+k])[0,1] for k in (-2,-1,0,1,2)}
    tbl = pd.DataFrame(res, columns=["Area A used (km²)", "r (daily)", "bias of file vs USGS", "RMSE (mm/d)"])
    print(f"n = {len(common):,} daily pairs, {common[0].date()} … {common[-1].date()} (calibration window only)")
    print(f"Least-squares effective area  A = {A_ls:.1f} km²")
    print("Day-shift test  r(lag): " + ", ".join(f"{k:+d} d → {v:.4f}" for k, v in lags.items()))
    display(tbl.style.hide(axis="index"))
else:
    print("network unavailable; VERIFIED values obtained 2026-09-15: n = 13,515 daily pairs, "
          "A_ls = 1949.2 km², r = 1.000000, bias 0.00 %, RMSE 0.0010 mm/d; "

Conclusions for a02 (all VERIFIED):

Q is mm/day, not m³/s. The conversion actually used by the NWS when the file was built is Q_mm = Q_m3s · 86.4 / 1949.1 km² (= Q_cfs · 0.0283168 · 86.4 / 1949.1 = Q_cfs · 0.00125523). Using the NWIS area 1924.4 km² would give a +1.3 % bias, using the literature 1944 km² a +0.26 % bias.
The record starts 1948-10-01: with that alignment, daily r = 1.000000 against USGS; shifting the calendar by ±265 or ±365 days destroys the correspondence (water-year means: r drops from 1.00000 to 0.35 / 0.11). This is independent confirmation of the ISSUE-001 resolution (periods.definition: dates).
Q at this gauge has no missing days in 1951-10-01…1988-09-30, and GAGES-II reports only 0.6 % estimated values over the whole record (Falcone 2011) — so data quality is not a limiting factor.

Figure 3: Budyko diagram. The Leaf River basin (calibration window of the modelling file, and the independent PRISM/Hamon + Wolock-McCabe runoff estimate) plots close to, but slightly above, the Budyko curve: it evaporates a little more (or yields a little less runoff) than the energy/water limits alone would predict — consistent with dense pine forest, 13.6 % woody wetland and deep sandy soils.





file      : phi = 0.742, E/P = 0.654, runoff ratio = 0.346 (Budyko-expected E/P = 0.583)
GAGES-II  : phi = 0.627, E/P = 0.629, runoff ratio = 0.371


The basin is energy-limited but only just (φ ≈ 0.63–0.74): in an average year ~65 % of precipitation is evaporated and ~35 % becomes runoff. The point sits ~0.07 above the Budyko curve, i.e. actual ET is ~10 % higher than the curve suggests. Modelling implications: actual ET must be allowed to approach PET when the soil is wet (no strong global ET reduction factor), and an annual water balance closure of P − E − Q ≈ 0 with E/P ≈ 0.65 is the correct long-term target (a KGE β close to 1 requires it).

This is the most important table for parameter priors. Three consequences:

65 % of the basin is hydrologic soil group C or D. Infiltration capacity at the surface is moderate to low even though the parent material is sandy — a silty/clayey surface horizon over sand. Therefore both infiltration-excess (during intense summer convective storms) and saturation-excess (winter, valley bottoms) runoff occur. GAGES-II carries Wolock’s split explicitly: Horton overland flow 7.1 %, Dunne (saturation) overland flow 5.1 % of the basin’s runoff generation. Neither dominates, and together they explain only ~12 % ⇒ ~88 % of streamflow leaves the hillslope through the subsurface.
Plant-available soil storage ≈ 230 mm (0.15 mm/mm × 1516 mm). For a lumped conceptual store this is the right order for the mean capacity; spatially distributed formulations (HYMOD/PDM Cmax, GR4J x1) need a maximum 2–4× larger. Recommended priors in §10.
Water table at ~1.1 m and 13.6 % woody wetland ⇒ riparian saturated areas are always close to the surface: a variable-contributing-area formulation (β/b-exponent > 0) is physically justified.

text:
7.2 Recession, baseflow and the flow-duration curve


Code
Pc = cm["P"].to_numpy()

def lyne_hollick(x, a=0.925, passes=3):
    y = x.copy()
    for p in range(passes):
        if p % 2: y = y[::-1]
        f = np.zeros_like(y); f[0] = y[0]
        for i in range(1, len(y)):
            f[i] = a*f[i-1] + (1+a)/2*(y[i]-y[i-1])
        b = np.minimum(y, y - np.maximum(f, 0))
        if p % 2: b = b[::-1]; y = y[::-1]
        y = b
    return y

bf   = lyne_hollick(q); BFI  = bf.sum()/q.sum()
bf98 = lyne_hollick(q, a=0.98); BFI98 = bf98.sum()/q.sum()
lags = np.arange(0, 11)
xcorr = [np.corrcoef(Pc[:len(Pc)-k], q[k:])[0, 1] for k in lags]
dry = np.ones(len(q), bool)
for k in range(3): dry[k:] &= (Pc[:len(Pc)-k] < 0.5)

ratio = ratio[(ratio > 0.3) & (ratio < 1.0)]

Three independent estimates agree on a catchment response time of 1–3 days, with the storage response (τ ≈ 11 d for the slow store) an order of magnitude longer. The daily time step therefore resolves the routing only marginally: a Nash cascade of 2–3 linear reservoirs, a GR4J-type unit hydrograph with x4 ≈ 1.5–3 d, or a 1–2 day pure lag are all defensible; a full hydraulic routing scheme is not.

The evaluation window WY1949–WY1951 is shaded: it contains the January 1950 flood (45,400 ft³/s ≈ 57 mm/d instantaneous), the 3rd largest peak of the 1939–1988 systematic record.





Largest systematic peaks 1939–1988 (ft³/s): 1974-04-14 54,200, 1961-02-23 48,500, 1950-01-08 45,400, 1979-03-05 36,900, 1980-04-14 31,300

Floods are winter–spring, frontal events: of the 50 annual peaks 1939–1988, 48 occur between December and May (27 in March–April alone), 2 in October and none in June–September. Summer convective and even tropical-cyclone rain rarely produces the annual maximum, because the soil store is empty — another strong argument for a state-dependent runoff-generation function.
Largest events of the modelling record: 1974-04-14 (54,200 ft³/s), 1961-02-23 (48,500), 1950-01-08 (45,400), 1990-02-17 (46,700, outside); historic 1856-04 (56,000).
The evaluation window (WY1949–WY1951) contains one of the largest floods of the century (Jan 1950) and, per the scaffold note, is wetter than the calibration mean. Models that extrapolate badly on the upper tail (e.g. saturating storage, hard Cmax ceilings) will be penalised there. Recommendation to a03: prefer structures whose fast-runoff function has no hard upper bound, and to a10: do not let the calibration force Cmax/x1 to the lower edge of its prior.
Low flows: the 7-day minimum never reaches zero; October is the driest month (13.6 mm of runoff). A model that drains its groundwater store to zero in autumn will lose KGE through the variability ratio.

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
section: 3.3 Why these five, and what was rejected
text:
3.3 Why these five, and what was rejected
Selected: ARX–API ridge (slot 1), GR4J (2), HBV-light without snow (3), SAC-SMA without Snow-17 (4), single-basin LSTM (5).
The screening is not a pure ranking exercise: slot 1 is included by design even though HYMOD scores marginally higher (3.90 vs 3.84). A statistical lower benchmark is mandatory for the project’s central question (“does complexity pay off?”) — without it the gradient has no origin — and its low process score is precisely the point. Everything above slot 1 in the screening that is not selected is rejected for the reasons below.
Rejections and overrides, with reasons:

HYMOD is not used, although it is the historical Leaf River model (Boyle et al. 2000; Vrugt et al. 2003). The skill’s default set proposes it; I override it and log the decision. HYMOD routes its slow response through a single linear reservoir, which is exactly the structure a02 falsifies (\(b = 1.68 \ne 1\), and 9-d vs 549-d time scales). Its production store is a Moore PDM (Moore 1985), i.e. conceptually the same variable-contributing-area idea already carried by GR4J’s production store and HBV’s \(\beta\) function, so it would add little complementarity at 5 parameters — a slot almost identical in complexity to GR4J’s 4. Replacing it with HBV-light buys (i) an explicit threshold UZL in the fast response, (ii) two subsurface time scales, (iii) the best documented at-gauge conceptual score (NSE 0.819, a01), and (iv) it fills the complexity gap between 4 and 15 parameters. The historical Leaf River lineage is preserved through SAC-SMA, which is the model of Duan et al. (1992), Sorooshian et al. (1993) and Boyle et al. (2000) on this very record.
TOPMODEL requires a topographic-index distribution; a01 only provides a single GAGES-II TWI value (12.69), so the index histogram would have to be invented. Rejected on data demands.
Xinanjiang / PDM / FUSE / MARRMoT score well on process but add nothing that SAC-SMA + HBV do not already cover, and FUSE/MARRMoT would mean porting a framework (high implementation risk in one session).
Gradient boosting / GRU / TCN: a tree ensemble cannot carry state, so it needs the same hand-made antecedent features as slot 1 while losing the closed-form transparency; GRU/TCN are near-duplicates of the LSTM with less hydrological literature. Rejected on complementarity.
dPL / differentiable hybrid (Feng et al. 2022) scores highest on process and complementarity but has the worst implementation risk (a torch time-stepping loop with smoothed thresholds, trained jointly with a network, written blind by one agent in one session) and the worst compute score. The hybrid idea is not lost: it re-enters as the pre-declared ensembles ens_physics_plus_ml and ens_best_conceptual_plus_lstm (Section 12), which a16 evaluates with weights fixed on calibration data only — the same scientific question at a fraction of the risk.

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
5.1 Overview
A persistence-free linear model: the predictors are non-linear functions of the forcing only (\(P\), \(PET\), day of year); no observed or simulated \(Q\) enters the right-hand side, so the comparison with the conceptual slots is fair (a catchment model also only sees \(P\) and \(PET\)). The two ideas that lift it above a naive regression are (i) antecedent precipitation indices (API), the oldest storage proxy in hydrology and the backbone of IHACRES-type models (Jakeman and Hornberger 1993), and (ii) a Box–Cox target transform (Box and Cox 1964) with a bias-corrected back-transform (Duan 1983), which handles the extreme skew of daily \(Q\) (a02: skew 6.85). Estimation is ridge regression (Hoerl and Kennard 1970), i.e. closed form, so one model evaluation costs one \(\sim 22 \times 22\) linear solve.
Why for the Leaf River. a02 shows that the \(R^2\) of a linear model on lagged \(P\) rises monotonically with the lag window (0.59 at 10 d → 0.65 at 365 d): most of the daily signal is input memory. This slot quantifies exactly how much, and thereby prices the conceptual structure of slots 2–4.

5.3 Perceptual → conceptual assumptions

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
5.6 Initial states and warm-up
\(A^{(j)}_{-1}=E^{\text{ant}}_{-1}=0\). With \(\lambda_{\text{slow}} \le 0.999\) the slowest recursion needs \(\approx 3/(1-\lambda) \approx 3000\) d to be fully spun up in the worst case, but \(\ge 365\) d removes >97 % of the transient for \(\lambda \le 0.992\); warmup_days_min: 365 is declared, and a11 must keep \(\lambda_{\text{slow}} \le 0.995\) if the evaluation warm-up (92 d) is a concern — the model is standardised, so a residual spin-up offset is largely absorbed by the intercept.

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
5.7 Mass balance check
Not applicable (no stores). The builder must instead assert, on the fitting window, \(0.9 \le \overline{\hat Q}/\overline{Q} \le 1.1\) (guaranteed by Equation 6 up to the clipping) and \(\hat Q_t > 0\;\forall t\).
crumbs: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
5.8 Numerical pitfalls

Standardise the design columns before the ridge solve, otherwise \(\alpha\) means something different for every column; store the means/sds in the artefact and reuse them at prediction time.
Use scipy.linalg.solve(A, b, assume_a="pos"), never np.linalg.inv.
Clip \(\lambda_{bc}y+1\) at \(10^{-9}\) before the fractional power (Equation 4), otherwise NaNs appear for strongly negative predictions.
n_lag arrives from a continuous optimizer: round it (int(round(x))) and clip to [1, 10].
The first n_lag rows of the frame have undefined lags: fill with 0 (dry) and exclude them from fitting.
crumbs: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
5.9 Implementation route
From scratch, numpy + scipy.linalg. kind: "trainable", so: fit(forcing, target, params) builds Equation 3, solves Equation 5 and stores \((\hat\beta, \text{col means/sds}, c, \lambda_{bc}, n_\ell)\); simulate(forcing, params) rebuilds the features on the frame it is given and applies the stored coefficients. Lazy-fit rule: if simulate is called on an unfitted instance it must fit itself on the calibration window obtained through src.common.data (never slice_run(..., "evaluation")) and emit a warning. save/load must round-trip a plain .npz/.json artefact.
Fitting protocol (also in config/models.yaml → fit_protocol): coefficients on calibration_internal.train, hyperparameters selected on calibration_internal.validation, then a final closed-form refit of the coefficients on the full calibration metric window with the selected hyperparameters. No evaluation data at any stage.

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
5.10 Expected behaviour
Strengths: unbiased in the mean by construction, extremely cheap, no equifinality drama, and a transparent statement of “how much is memory”. Weaknesses: no mass conservation, it will smear flood peaks (a linear map cannot produce a 45 mm/d spike from a 100 mm storm on dry soil), and recessions decay as a mixture of exponentials fixed by \(\lambda_j\) rather than by storage. Expected NSE 0.60–0.75 (calibration), 0.50–0.72 (evaluation); KGE \(\alpha\) clearly below 1 (variance under-dispersion).

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
6.1 Overview
GR4J (Perrin et al. 2003) is the four-parameter daily lumped model of the French “Génie Rural” family, developed by successive structural simplification tested on 429 catchments. It is the standard parsimony benchmark in comparative hydrology and is available as the R package airGR (Coron et al. 2017), which the builder should use as a numerical test oracle if R is available (it is not required). Wang and Gupta (2024) applied GR-type and other lumped structures to this very record.
Why for the Leaf River. GR4J satisfies four of the five hard requirements with four parameters: a soil-moisture-dependent production function (variable runoff coefficient), ET that can reach PET, a non-linear routing store with \(Q_r \propto R^5\) for small \(R\) — the direct analogue of the observed Brutsaert–Nieber \(b = 1.68\) — and a 1–3 d unit hydrograph. Its weak point here is that it has one slow store; the exchange term \(x_2\) then has to absorb the long-term balance, which makes it an interesting diagnostic (a01 flags inter-catchment exchange as a MEDIUM-priority process).

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
6.3 Perceptual → conceptual assumptions
Represented: soil-moisture control of the runoff coefficient (saturation-excess in a bulk sense), ET limited by soil water, percolation to a routing store, non-linear release, translation delay, and a net gain/loss of groundwater across the topographic divide. Ignored: separate tension/free water, an explicit second (very slow) aquifer, any snow or frozen ground, and a distinction between fast surface and fast subsurface flow.
crumbs: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
6.4 Mathematical formulation
State variables: \(S\) (production store, mm, \(0\le S\le x_1\)), \(R\) (routing store, mm, \(R\ge 0\)), plus the two unit-hydrograph memory vectors. Order of operations within day \(t\) (explicit, operator-split; this is the scheme actually used, not an ODE solver):
(1) Net forcing. With \(E = \mathrm{PET}_t\): \[P_n = \max(P_t - E,\,0),\qquad E_n = \max(E - P_t,\,0) \quad(\text{only one is non-zero}) \tag{7}\]
(2) Rain entering the production store. \[P_s = \frac{x_1\left(1-\left(\frac{S}{x_1}\right)^2\right)\tanh\!\frac{P_n}{x_1}}
{1+\frac{S}{x_1}\tanh\!\frac{P_n}{x_1}} \tag{8}\]
(3) Actual evaporation from the store. \[E_s = \frac{S\left(2-\frac{S}{x_1}\right)\tanh\!\frac{E_n}{x_1}}
{1+\left(1-\frac{S}{x_1}\right)\tanh\!\frac{E_n}{x_1}} \tag{9}\]
(4) Store update. \(\;S \leftarrow S - E_s + P_s\).
(5) Percolation. \[\mathrm{Perc} = S\left[1-\left(1+\left(\tfrac{4}{9}\tfrac{S}{x_1}\right)^{4}\right)^{-1/4}\right],
\qquad S \leftarrow S - \mathrm{Perc} \tag{10}\]
(6) Routed volume. \(\;P_r = \mathrm{Perc} + (P_n - P_s)\), split 90 % / 10 %.
(7) Unit hydrographs. With \(\mathrm{SH}_1(u)=0\) for \(u\le0\), \((u/x_4)^{5/2}\) for \(0<u<x_4\), \(1\) for \(u\ge x_4\); and \(\mathrm{SH}_2(u)= \tfrac12 (u/x_4)^{5/2}\) for \(0<u<x_4\), \(1-\tfrac12(2-u/x_4)^{5/2}\) for \(x_4\le u<2x_4\), \(1\) for \(u\ge 2x_4\): \[u^{(1)}_j = \mathrm{SH}_1(j)-\mathrm{SH}_1(j-1),\quad j=1..\lceil x_4\rceil;\qquad
u^{(2)}_j = \mathrm{SH}_2(j)-\mathrm{SH}_2(j-1),\quad j=1..\lceil 2x_4\rceil \tag{11}\] \[Q_9 = 0.9\sum_j u^{(1)}_j P_r(t-j+1),\qquad Q_1 = 0.1\sum_j u^{(2)}_j P_r(t-j+1) \tag{12}\]
(8) Groundwater exchange. \(\;F = x_2\left(\dfrac{R}{x_3}\right)^{7/2}\)
(9) Routing store. \(\;R \leftarrow \max(0,\;R + Q_9 + F)\), then \[Q_r = R\left[1-\left(1+\left(\tfrac{R}{x_3}\right)^{4}\right)^{-1/4}\right],\qquad R \leftarrow R - Q_r \tag{13}\]
(10) Output. \(\;Q_d = \max(0,\,Q_1+F)\), \(\;\boxed{Q_t = Q_r + Q_d}\)
For small \(R/x_3\), Equation 13 expands to \(Q_r \approx R^5/(4x_3^4)\): a strongly non-linear storage–discharge relation, which is precisely why GR4J can reproduce a \(b>1\) recession with a single store.

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
6.7 Mass balance check (builder must test)
Accumulating over any window, \[\sum P - \sum E_s - \sum Q \;+\; \sum F^{\text{added}} \;=\; \Delta S + \Delta R + \Delta \mathrm{UH}_1 + \Delta \mathrm{UH}_2 \tag{14}\] where \(F^{\text{added}}\) is the exchange water actually added (i.e. after the \(\max(0,\cdot)\) clips in steps 9 and 10, counted once for the routing branch and once for the direct branch). Required tolerance: \(|\text{residual}| < 10^{-8}\) mm per 1000 days. Run the test with \(x_2=0\) first (then \(F\equiv0\) and the identity is exact), then with \(x_2=\pm3\) mm/d.

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
6.8 Numerical pitfalls

\(\tanh\) overflows for arguments \(\gtrsim 20\); clip \(P_n/x_1\) and \(E_n/x_1\) at 13.
\(\sum_j u^{(1)}_j = \sum_j u^{(2)}_j = 1\) must hold to \(10^{-12}\); recompute ordinates whenever \(x_4\) changes (i.e. once per parameter set, not per time step).
\(\lceil x_4\rceil\) with \(x_4 = 1.0\) gives a single ordinate — make sure the array is never empty (bounds start at 0.5, so \(\lceil x_4\rceil\ge1\) always).
With \(x_2<0\) the routing store can be driven negative: clip and record the clipped amount for



Keep \(S\) inside \([0,x_1]\) by construction (Equation 8–Equation 9 guarantee it analytically); add an assertion rather than a clip, so a coding error is caught instead of hidden.

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
6.9 Implementation route
From scratch, NumPy with an explicit daily loop (optionally numba.njit); ~40 lines. Follow Perrin et al. (2003) Appendix and the airGR::RunModel_GR4J reference (Coron et al. 2017). Validate on (i) the mass balance above, (ii) a 1-day impulse: a single 100 mm rain on a dry store must produce a hydrograph whose peak is at day \(\approx x_4\) and whose volume equals the routed volume, and (iii) if R is available, airGR output agreement to \(10^{-6}\) mm/d.

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
6.10 Expected behaviour
Strengths: robust, few parameters, very fast (\(10^5\) runs are cheap), non-linear recession, excellent prior evidence on humid catchments. Weaknesses: a single slow store must serve both the 10-d and the several-hundred-day time scale, so expect systematic under-estimation of very long summer recessions; \(x_2\) may compensate a structural ET error and end up physically implausible (watch \(|x_2|>3\) mm/d). Expected NSE 0.78–0.86 (calibration), 0.72–0.84 (evaluation).

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
7.1 Overview
HBV (Bergström 1992; Lindström et al. 1997) in the “HBV-light” formulation of Seibert and Vis (2012), with the snow routine removed (a01 decision: snow = 0.8 % of \(P\); DECISIONS.md). Nine parameters: three for the soil routine, five for the response routine, one for routing. HBV is the best-performing conceptual model documented at this gauge (calibrated NSE 0.819; uncalibrated 0.687 — a01, after Kratzert et al. (2019)).
Why for the Leaf River. It is the only structure in the portfolio with an explicit storage threshold in the fast response: the outlet \(K_0\) only operates when \(S_{UZ} > UZL\). a02’s event analysis (runoff coefficients spanning two orders of magnitude and correlated with antecedent wetness, \(r = 0.57\)) is exactly the signature of a threshold. It also carries the two subsurface time scales demanded by Section 2 (\(K_1 \approx 0.1\) d⁻¹ ⇒ \(\tau \approx 10\) d; \(K_2 \approx 0.002\) d⁻¹ ⇒ \(\tau \approx 500\) d), and its \(\beta\)-function recharge is a different parameterisation of the variable contributing area than GR4J’s \(\tanh\) production store — good for ensemble diversity.

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
7.3 Perceptual → conceptual assumptions
Represented: a non-linear (power-law) partition of rain between soil storage and recharge; ET throttled below a soil-moisture threshold \(LP\cdot FC\); a capped percolation to a deep store; a threshold-activated near-surface outlet, an interflow outlet and a slow baseflow outlet; translation by a symmetric triangle. Ignored: tension/free-water distinction, capillary rise (the optional HBV CFLUX term is dropped), groundwater exchange across the divide, and any land-cover zonation (the basin is run as one lumped zone).
crumbs: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
7.4 Mathematical formulation
States: \(SM\) (mm, \(0\le SM\le FC\)), \(S_{UZ}\) (mm), \(S_{LZ}\) (mm), and the MAXBAS memory. Order of operations within day \(t\) (explicit Euler / operator splitting):
(1) Recharge (soil routine). \[R_t = P_t\left(\frac{SM_{t-1}}{FC}\right)^{\beta},\qquad SM^{*} = SM_{t-1} + P_t - R_t \tag{15}\] If \(SM^{*} > FC\), move the excess to recharge: \(R_t \leftarrow R_t + (SM^{*}-FC)\), \(SM^{*} \leftarrow FC\).
(2) Actual evaporation. \[E_{a,t} = \mathrm{PET}_t \cdot \min\!\left(\frac{SM^{*}}{LP\cdot FC},\,1\right),\qquad
SM_t = \max\!\big(SM^{*} - E_{a,t},\,0\big) \tag{16}\] (if the \(\max\) clips, reduce \(E_{a,t}\) by the clipped amount so mass is conserved).
(3) Percolation. \[\mathrm{PERC}_t = \min\big(\mathrm{PERC},\; S_{UZ,t-1} + R_t\big),\qquad
S^{*}_{UZ} = S_{UZ,t-1} + R_t - \mathrm{PERC}_t,\qquad
S^{*}_{LZ} = S_{LZ,t-1} + \mathrm{PERC}_t \tag{17}\]
(4) Response routine (with the effective constants \(K_0^{\text{eff}}=\max(K_0,K_1)\) and \(K_2^{\text{eff}}=\min(K_2,\,0.9K_1)\), see Section 7.5): \[Q_{0,t}=K_0^{\text{eff}}\max\!\big(S^{*}_{UZ}-UZL,\,0\big),\qquad
Q_{1,t}=K_1 S^{*}_{UZ},\qquad
Q_{2,t}=K_2^{\text{eff}} S^{*}_{LZ} \tag{18}\] \[S_{UZ,t} = S^{*}_{UZ}-Q_{0,t}-Q_{1,t},\qquad S_{LZ,t}=S^{*}_{LZ}-Q_{2,t} \tag{19}\] If \(Q_{0,t}+Q_{1,t} > S^{*}_{UZ}\) (possible only for extreme \(K\) combinations), scale both down by \(S^{*}_{UZ}/(Q_{0,t}+Q_{1,t})\) and set \(S_{UZ,t}=0\).
(5) Routing. Generated runoff \(Q^{\text{gen}}_t = Q_{0,t}+Q_{1,t}+Q_{2,t}\) is convolved with the triangular weights obtained by integrating the unit-area isosceles triangle \(h(u)\) on \([0,\mathrm{MAXBAS}]\): \[w_j=\int_{j-1}^{j} h(u)\,\mathrm{d}u,\quad j=1..\lceil \mathrm{MAXBAS}\rceil,\qquad
h(u)=\frac{4}{\mathrm{MAXBAS}^2}\min\!\big(u,\ \mathrm{MAXBAS}-u\big)_+  \tag{20}\] \[w_j \leftarrow w_j\Big/\sum_k w_k,\qquad \boxed{\,Q_t=\sum_j w_j\,Q^{\text{gen}}_{t-j+1}\,} \tag{21}\]

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
7.5 Parameter ordering rule
HBV requires \(K_0 \ge K_1 > K_2\). Rectangular bounds are far easier for a global optimizer, so the model enforces the ordering by the monotone maps \(K_0^{\text{eff}}=\max(K_0,K_1)\), \(K_2^{\text{eff}}=\min(K_2,0.9K_1)\). The optimizer therefore searches a box; the effective values must be reported by a13 alongside the raw ones.

7.8 Mass balance check (builder must test)
\[\sum P - \sum E_a - \sum Q \;=\; \Delta SM + \Delta S_{UZ} + \Delta S_{LZ} + \Delta \mathrm{UH} \tag{22}\] with \(|\text{residual}| < 10^{-8}\) mm per 1000 days. HBV has no exchange term, so this identity is exact and is the strongest single test of the implementation.

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River

7.9 Numerical pitfalls

Compute the recharge with \(SM_{t-1}\) (start-of-step storage), then update — swapping the order changes the model.
Cap \(SM\) at \(FC\) by transferring the excess to \(R_t\); never discard it.
\(\left(SM/FC\right)^\beta\) with \(SM=0\) is 0 for \(\beta\ge1\) — fine, but guard \(SM\ge0\) anyway.
Fluxes in Equation 18 are computed from the pre-update storages; subtract afterwards (explicit Euler).
Normalise the MAXBAS weights (Equation 21): the analytic integral of the truncated triangle does not sum to 1 when \(\mathrm{MAXBAS}\) is not an integer.
PERC = 0 is inside the bounds and legal (then \(S_{LZ}\) only drains) — do not divide by it.

7.11 Expected behaviour
Strengths: explicit threshold response, two subsurface time scales, strong at-gauge evidence, still cheap enough for \(10^5\) runs. Weaknesses: the lower box is linear, so the very-long-tail recession is exponential rather than power-law; \(UZL\)/\(K_0\) are typically weakly identified in a basin with only 12 % overland flow, so expect a flat likelihood ridge there (a10: this pair is the main equifinality risk). Expected NSE 0.80–0.87 (calibration), 0.74–0.85 (evaluation).

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
8.1 Overview
The Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting model (Burnash et al. 1973) is the US National Weather Service River Forecast System’s operational rainfall–runoff model, and the historical test bed of this very data set: Duan et al. (1992) introduced SCE-UA by calibrating SAC-SMA on the Leaf River, Sorooshian et al. (1993) studied its data requirements here, and Boyle et al. (2000) its multi-criteria calibration. a01 reports NSE 0.796 for a calibrated SAC-SMA + Snow-17 at 02472000.
Why for the Leaf River. It is the only structure in the portfolio that represents all of a01’s process priorities simultaneously: (i) a tension/free-water split in both the upper and the lower zone (so ET can draw from tension water while free water drains), (ii) a variable contributing area (ADIMP) that saturates and generates direct runoff, matching the Dunne 5.1 % / wetland 13.6 % signature, (iii) a demand-driven percolation whose rate rises with lower-zone deficiency (\(\mathrm{ZPERC}\), \(\mathrm{REXP}\)) — a genuine non-linear coupling absent from GR4J and HBV, and (iv) two parallel baseflow stores (LZFSC, LZFPC) with independent depletion rates, the direct representation of the 9-d vs 549-d puzzle. Snow-17 is omitted (a01 decision).

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
8.3 Perceptual → conceptual assumptions
Represented: infiltration-excess (via PCTIM/upper-zone overflow), saturation-excess on an expanding area (ADIMP), interflow, two baseflow components, tension-water ET demand hierarchy, and storage-deficiency-driven percolation. Ignored: snow, riparian ET (RIVA = 0), deep recharge that bypasses the gauge (SIDE = 0), and any spatial distribution.
crumbs: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
8.4 Mathematical formulation
States (mm): \(UZTWC, UZFWC, LZTWC, LZFSC, LZFPC, ADIMC\) and the UH memory. Derived constant: \(\mathrm{PAREA} = 1 - \mathrm{PCTIM} - \mathrm{ADIMP}\). The algorithm below is the NWS fland1 sequence; it must be implemented exactly in this order.
(4.1) Evapotranspiration demand hierarchy. With \(E_{\text{dmnd}} = \mathrm{PET}_t\): \[E_1 = E_{\text{dmnd}}\frac{UZTWC}{UZTWM},\qquad UZTWC \leftarrow UZTWC - E_1,\qquad
\mathrm{RED} = E_{\text{dmnd}}-E_1\] (if \(UZTWC<0\): \(E_1 \leftarrow E_1 + UZTWC\), \(UZTWC \leftarrow 0\)) \[E_2 = \min(\mathrm{RED},\,UZFWC),\qquad UZFWC \leftarrow UZFWC-E_2,\qquad \mathrm{RED}\leftarrow \mathrm{RED}-E_2\] Upper-zone rebalance: if \(UZTWC/UZTWM < UZFWC/UZFWM\), set \(\mathrm{UZRAT}=\dfrac{UZTWC+UZFWC}{UZTWM+UZFWM}\), \(UZTWC = UZTWM\cdot \mathrm{UZRAT}\), \(UZFWC = UZFWM\cdot \mathrm{UZRAT}\). \[E_3 = \mathrm{RED}\,\frac{LZTWC}{UZTWM+LZTWM},\qquad LZTWC \leftarrow LZTWC - E_3 \;(\ge 0) \tag{23}\] Lower-zone tension resupply: with \(\mathrm{SAVED}=\mathrm{RSERV}(LZFPM+LZFSM)\), \(\mathrm{RATLZT}=LZTWC/LZTWM\) and \(\mathrm{RATLZ}=\dfrac{LZTWC+LZFPC+LZFSC-\mathrm{SAVED}}{LZTWM+LZFPM+LZFSM-\mathrm{SAVED}}\): if \(\mathrm{RATLZT}<\mathrm{RATLZ}\), transfer \(\mathrm{DEL}=(\mathrm{RATLZ}-\mathrm{RATLZT})LZTWM\) from \(LZFSC\) (then \(LZFPC\) if \(LZFSC\) runs out) to \(LZTWC\). ET from the additional impervious area: \[E_5 = E_1 + (\mathrm{RED}+E_2)\frac{ADIMC-E_1-UZTWC}{UZTWM+LZTWM},\qquad ADIMC\leftarrow ADIMC-E_5\;(\ge0),
\qquad E_5 \leftarrow \mathrm{ADIMP}\cdot E_5 \tag{24}\]
(4.2) Precipitation into the upper tension store. \[\mathrm{TWX}=\max(P_t + UZTWC - UZTWM,\,0),\qquad
UZTWC = \begin{cases}UZTWC+P_t & \text{if } P_t+UZTWC<UZTWM\\ UZTWM & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}\] \[ADIMC \leftarrow ADIMC + P_t - \mathrm{TWX},\qquad \mathrm{ROIMP}=P_t\cdot \mathrm{PCTIM} \tag{25}\]
(4.3) Sub-daily incrementation (mandatory for stability): \[N_{\text{inc}} = 1+\left\lfloor 0.2\,(UZFWC+\mathrm{TWX})\right\rfloor,\quad
\Delta = 1/N_{\text{inc}},\quad P_{\text{inc}}=\mathrm{TWX}/N_{\text{inc}}\] \[D_{UZ}=1-(1-\mathrm{UZK})^{\Delta},\quad D_{LZP}=1-(1-\mathrm{LZPK})^{\Delta},\quad
D_{LZS}=1-(1-\mathrm{LZSK})^{\Delta} \tag{26}\]
(4.4) Loop \(i=1..N_{\text{inc}}\):

Additional-impervious direct runoff. \(\mathrm{RATIO}=\max\!\big((ADIMC-UZTWC)/LZTWM,\,0\big)\), \(\;\mathrm{ADDRO}=P_{\text{inc}}\mathrm{RATIO}^2\).
Baseflow. \(B_p = LZFPC\,D_{LZP}\), \(LZFPC \mathrel{-}= B_p\); \(B_s = LZFSC\,D_{LZS}\), \(LZFSC \mathrel{-}= B_s\); accumulate \(\mathrm{SBF} \mathrel{+}= B_p+B_s\).
Percolation (only if \(P_{\text{inc}}+UZFWC>2\cdot10^{-6}\)): \[\mathrm{PERCM}=LZFPM\,D_{LZP}+LZFSM\,D_{LZS},\qquad
\mathrm{DEFR}=1-\frac{LZTWC+LZFPC+LZFSC}{LZTWM+LZFPM+LZFSM}\] \[\mathrm{PERC}=\mathrm{PERCM}\Big(1+\mathrm{ZPERC}\,\mathrm{DEFR}^{\mathrm{REXP}}\Big)\frac{UZFWC}{UZFWM} \tag{27}\] capped by \(\mathrm{PERC}\le UZFWC\) and by the remaining remaining lower-zone capacity; then \(UZFWC \mathrel{-}= \mathrm{PERC}\).
Interflow. \(\;\mathrm{DEL}=UZFWC\,D_{UZ}\), \(\;\mathrm{SIF}\mathrel{+}=\mathrm{DEL}\), \(\;UZFWC\mathrel{-}=\mathrm{DEL}\).
Distribute percolation. \(\mathrm{PERCT}=\mathrm{PERC}(1-\mathrm{PFREE})\) goes to \(LZTWC\) (overflow \(\mathrm{PERCF}\) carries on); \(\mathrm{PERCF}\mathrel{+}=\mathrm{PERC}\cdot\mathrm{PFREE}\). Split \(\mathrm{PERCF}\) between the two free-water stores with \[\mathrm{HPL}=\frac{LZFPM}{LZFPM+LZFSM},\quad
\mathrm{FRACP}=\min\!\left(1,\ \mathrm{HPL}\,\frac{2(1-LZFPC/LZFPM)}{(1-LZFPC/LZFPM)+(1-LZFSC/LZFSM)}\right) \tag{28}\] \(\mathrm{PERCP}=\mathrm{FRACP}\cdot\mathrm{PERCF}\) → \(LZFPC\), remainder → \(LZFSC\); any overflow of either store is returned to \(LZTWC\).
Surface runoff. If \(P_{\text{inc}}+UZFWC>UZFWM\): \(\mathrm{SUR}=P_{\text{inc}}+UZFWC-UZFWM\), \(UZFWC=UZFWM\), \(\mathrm{SSUR}\mathrel{+}=\mathrm{SUR}\cdot \mathrm{PAREA}\), \(\mathrm{ADSUR}=\mathrm{SUR}\left(1-\mathrm{ADDRO}/P_{\text{inc}}\right)\), \(\mathrm{SSUR}\mathrel{+}=\mathrm{ADSUR}\cdot\mathrm{ADIMP}\); else \(UZFWC\mathrel{+}=P_{\text{inc}}\), \(\mathrm{ADSUR}=0\).
ADIMC update. \(ADIMC \mathrel{+}= P_{\text{inc}}-\mathrm{ADDRO}-\mathrm{ADSUR}\); if \(ADIMC>UZTWM+LZTWM\), move the excess to \(\mathrm{ADDRO}\) and cap. Accumulate \(\mathrm{SDRO}\mathrel{+}=\mathrm{ADDRO}\cdot\mathrm{ADIMP}\).

(4.5) Channel inflow. \[\mathrm{TCI}_t = \mathrm{ROIMP} + \mathrm{SDRO} + \mathrm{SSUR} + \mathrm{SIF}\cdot \mathrm{PAREA}
+ \frac{\mathrm{SBF}\cdot \mathrm{PAREA}}{1+\mathrm{SIDE}} \tag{29}\] with \(\mathrm{SIDE}=0\) here. Total ET: \(\mathrm{TET}_t=(E_1+E_2+E_3)\mathrm{PAREA}+E_5\) (plus \(E_4=0\) since \(\mathrm{RIVA}=0\)).
(4.6) Routing — 2-parameter gamma (Nash) unit hydrograph (Nash 1957): \[u_j = F_\Gamma\!\big(j;\,\mathrm{UH\_N},\mathrm{UH\_K}\big)-F_\Gamma\!\big(j-1;\,\mathrm{UH\_N},\mathrm{UH\_K}\big),
\qquad j = 1..n_{uh},\qquad u_j \leftarrow u_j\Big/\textstyle\sum_k u_k \tag{30}\] \[\boxed{\,Q_t=\sum_{j=1}^{n_{uh}} u_j\,\mathrm{TCI}_{t-j+1}\,},\qquad
n_{uh}=\min\!\big(60,\ \min\{n: F_\Gamma(n)\ge0.9999\}\big)\] Mean lag \(=\mathrm{UH\_N}\cdot\mathrm{UH\_K}\) days, which the bounds place at 0.1–15 d with a prior of 1–3 d (a01).

\(UZTWC=0.5\,UZTWM\), \(UZFWC=0.1\,UZFWM\), \(LZTWC=0.6\,LZTWM\), \(LZFSC=0.2\,LZFSM\), \(LZFPC=0.6\,LZFPM\), \(ADIMC=UZTWC+LZTWC\) (a required consistency condition), UH memory zero. 8.7 Mass balance check (builder must test)
\[\sum P - \sum \mathrm{TET} - \sum \mathrm{TCI} \;=\;
\mathrm{PAREA}\,\Delta\!\left(UZTWC+UZFWC+LZTWC+LZFSC+LZFPC\right) + \mathrm{ADIMP}\,\Delta ADIMC
+ \Delta \mathrm{UH} \tag{31}\] Tolerance \(10^{-6}\) mm per 1000 days. Test it with \(\mathrm{PCTIM}=\mathrm{ADIMP}=0\) first (then \(\mathrm{PAREA}=1\) and the identity simplifies), then with \(\mathrm{ADIMP}=0.3\).

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
8.8 Numerical pitfalls

Never skip the sub-daily incrementation (Equation 26). With a 100 mm/d storm (the record maximum is 221.5 mm/d, a02) a single explicit step drains the upper zone by more than its content.
Convert depletion rates with \(1-(1-K)^{\Delta}\), not \(K\Delta\).
Guard every store: if abs(x) < 1e-10: x = 0, and return the clipped amount to the flux that caused it.
Assert \(UZTWC \le ADIMC \le UZTWM+LZTWM\) every step; violating it is the classic SAC-SMA coding bug.
In step (f) \(\mathrm{ADDRO}/P_{\text{inc}}\) divides by zero when \(P_{\text{inc}}=0\); that branch is only reached when \(P_{\text{inc}}>0\), but code the guard explicitly.
\(\mathrm{DEFR}\) can be slightly negative from round-off → max(DEFR, 0) before the power in Equation 27 (\(\mathrm{REXP}\) may be fractional).
Equation 28 divides by \((1-LZFPC/LZFPM)+(1-LZFSC/LZFSM)\), which is 0 when both stores are full; guard with \(\max(\cdot,10^{-9})\) and clamp \(\mathrm{FRACP}\in[0,1]\).
numba.njit the daily loop; a pure-Python loop is ~100× too slow for \(10^4\)–\(10^5\) optimizer runs (Section 11).

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
8.9 Implementation route
From scratch, NumPy + numba.njit, following Burnash et al. (1973) and the NWS fland1 ordering reproduced above; ~200 lines. Use scipy.stats.gamma.cdf once per parameter set for Equation 30. config/project.yaml carries external_references.sacsma_numba_path (currently null); if the user later supplies an existing Numba SAC-SMA, a08 should use it only as a test oracle, not as the deliverable. Validation: (i) Equation 31; (ii) with \(\mathrm{ADIMP}=\mathrm{PCTIM}=0\) and a 200-day dry spell the recession must be the sum of two exponentials with rates \(\mathrm{LZSK}\) and \(\mathrm{LZPK}\); (iii) simulated BFI (Lyne–Hollick, \(\alpha = 0.925\), 3 passes) with default parameters should land in 0.3–0.6.

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
8.10 Expected behaviour
Strengths: the most complete process representation available on P/PET alone; two baseflow time scales; the only structure able to separate “soil is wet but not saturated” from “saturated area is expanding”. Weaknesses: 15 parameters with well-documented equifinality (a01: LZPK-type parameters are the classic ill-identified ones here; Sorooshian et al. (1993)), a rough response surface (thresholds and the \(N_{\text{inc}}\) switch make it non-smooth → derivative-free global search only, see Section 15), and ~4× the run time of GR4J. Expected NSE 0.82–0.88 (calibration), 0.74–0.85 (evaluation).

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
9.1 Overview
A Long Short-Term Memory network (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997) applied to rainfall–runoff modelling following Kratzert et al. (2018) and Kratzert et al. (2019). The LSTM’s cell state acts as a learned, multi-dimensional storage system whose “recharge” and “release” are gated by the forcing — conceptually the same role as the stores in slots 2–4, but with the partitioning learned rather than prescribed. Kratzert et al. (2019) report NSE 0.84–0.86 for a regional LSTM at this exact gauge; here we have only one basin, so the design is heavily regularised.
Why for the Leaf River. (i) It is the only family in the portfolio whose errors are not generated by a prescribed store-and-release structure, which is what makes the ensembles in Section 12 worth testing. (ii) a02’s memory analysis (linear \(R^2\) still rising at a 365-day lag) says the basin has exactly the kind of long, non-linear memory an LSTM is built for. (iii) 36 calibration water years is at the lower edge of single-basin feasibility, which is why dropout, weight decay, early stopping and 5-seed averaging are all prescribed rather than optional.
