title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
9.3 Perceptual → conceptual assumptions
Represented: multi-scale memory of rainfall and evaporative demand, a learned non-linear wetness-dependent response, and seasonality (through PET and the harmonics). Ignored/absent: mass conservation, interpretable stores, any guarantee of behaviour outside the calibration input distribution. The evaluation window is 1.29× wetter in the mean than calibration but does not exceed the calibration flow magnitudes (a02), so the extrapolation risk is bounded but real.
crumbs: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
9.4 Mathematical formulation
Inputs. Base features (always): \[\mathbf{x}_t = \Big[\tfrac{P_t-3.9078}{10.1414},\;\tfrac{\mathrm{PET}_t-2.9004}{1.8890},\;
\sin\tfrac{2\pi d_t}{365.25},\;\cos\tfrac{2\pi d_t}{365.25}\Big] \tag{32}\] If use_antecedent_features = 1, ten more columns are appended: \(A^{(\lambda)}_t=\lambda A^{(\lambda)}_{t-1}+P_t\) for \(\lambda\in\{0.98,0.93,0.80\}\); \(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}P_{t-i}\) for \(k\in\{7,30,90,365\}\); and \(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(P_{t-i}-\mathrm{PET}_{t-i})\) for \(k\in\{30,90,365\}\). Each of these ten is standardised with its own mean/sd computed on the calibration metric window only and frozen in the model artefact.
Cell. Standard LSTM equations, with \(\sigma\) the logistic function and \(\odot\) the Hadamard product: \[\mathbf{i}_t=\sigma(W_i\mathbf{x}_t+U_i\mathbf{h}_{t-1}+\mathbf{b}_i),\qquad
\mathbf{f}_t=\sigma(W_f\mathbf{x}_t+U_f\mathbf{h}_{t-1}+\mathbf{b}_f) \tag{33}\] \[\mathbf{g}_t=\tanh(W_g\mathbf{x}_t+U_g\mathbf{h}_{t-1}+\mathbf{b}_g),\qquad
\mathbf{o}_t=\sigma(W_o\mathbf{x}_t+U_o\mathbf{h}_{t-1}+\mathbf{b}_o) \tag{34}\] \[\mathbf{c}_t=\mathbf{f}_t\odot\mathbf{c}_{t-1}+\mathbf{i}_t\odot\mathbf{g}_t,\qquad
\mathbf{h}_t=\mathbf{o}_t\odot\tanh(\mathbf{c}_t) \tag{35}\]
Head and output transform (\(\mu_Q=1.3533\), \(\sigma_Q=2.8511\) mm/d from the calibration window): \[\hat y_t=\mathbf{w}^\top \mathrm{Dropout}(\mathbf{h}_t)+b,\qquad
\boxed{\;\hat Q_t=\mathrm{softplus}\!\big(\mu_Q+\sigma_Q\,\hat y_t\big)=\ln\!\big(1+e^{\mu_Q+\sigma_Q\hat y_t}\big)\;} \tag{36}\] The softplus guarantees \(\hat Q_t>0\) (the river is perennial, a02) and keeps the gradient alive for the log-space loss term, which a hard clip would not.
Loss (\(\sigma_{\log Q}=1.2192\)): \[\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\left(\frac{\hat Q_t-Q_t}{\sigma_Q}\right)^{2}
\;+\;w_{\log}\,\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}
\left(\frac{\ln(\hat Q_t+10^{-6})-\ln Q_t}{\sigma_{\log Q}}\right)^{2} \tag{37}\] The first term is the NSE-equivalent objective on the reported metric; the second (weight \(w_{\log}\), default 0.25) protects the 40 % of days below 0.45 mm/d that the first term ignores (a02: the wettest 5 % of days carry 40 % of the volume). \(\mathcal{T}\) excludes the first warmup_steps of every training window.
Sequence handling. Training draws random contiguous windows of length seq_len (default 365 d) from the internal-train mask; the loss is evaluated only on steps \(t>\) warmup_steps (default 60), so the network learns to be accurate given as little as 60 days of context. At inference the model performs a single continuous forward pass over whatever frame simulate() receives, with \(\mathbf{h}_0=\mathbf{c}_0=\mathbf{0}\), emitting one \(\hat Q_t\) per day. This is what makes the LSTM comparable to the conceptual slots in the evaluation window, where only 92 warm-up days exist before the metric period begins (a01/a16 note).

9.7 Mass balance check
Not applicable. Required assertions instead: \(\hat Q_t>0\ \forall t\) and \(0.85\le\overline{\hat Q}/\overline{Q}\le1.15\) on the calibration metric window. a09 must additionally test that a continuous forward pass and a chunked pass with 365 d of context agree to \(<10^{-3}\) mm/d after the first 90 days — if they do not, the model has learned a state drift and seq_len must be raised.

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
9.8 Numerical pitfalls

Leakage: training windows must be drawn from internal_mask(frame, "train") only, and the standardisation constants must come from config/models.yaml → scaling: — never recomputed on the frame given at prediction time. load() must restore them; a silent re-standardisation on the evaluation frame would invalidate the whole study.
Use torch.nn.functional.softplus (numerically stable for large arguments), and \(\ln(\hat Q+10^{-6})\) in Equation 37.
MPS is not bit-reproducible for all kernels; set torch.manual_seed(seed) per member, and if the 5-member mean is not reproducible across runs, fall back to cpu and record it in the a09/a15 handoff (CLAUDE.md rule 7). Device via src.common.data.torch_device().
Round hidden_size, n_layers, seq_len, warmup_steps, batch_size, use_antecedent_features to integers when they arrive from a continuous optimizer.
The rolling 365-day features need 365 leading days; inside the evaluation frame those do not exist — compute them with a growing (partial) window and divide by the number of available days, i.e. pandas.Series.rolling(k, min_periods=1).mean() * k. Document the choice; it is applied identically in calibration and evaluation.
crumbs: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
9.9 Implementation route
torch 2.13.0 (BSD-3). kind: "trainable": fit(forcing, target, params) trains the 5 members; simulate(forcing, params) runs the continuous pass and averages them; save/load persist state_dicts + scaling constants + hyperparameters. Same lazy-fit rule as slot 1 (fit on the calibration window through src.common.data if unfitted; never on evaluation data). Compute budget: with 10,592 training days, seq_len 365 and batch 256 there are ~41 minibatches per epoch; at ≤200 epochs and 5 seeds this is well inside the 3 h limit (Section 11).

9.10 Expected behaviour
Strengths: the highest ceiling in the portfolio and a genuinely different error structure. Weaknesses: ~1.9 fitted weights per training day → overfitting is the main risk; no mass conservation, so the water-balance (\(\beta\)) term of KGE is not protected structurally; and behaviour in the wetter evaluation period is an empirical question. Expected NSE 0.85–0.92 (calibration), 0.75–0.87 (evaluation) — note the deliberately wide evaluation band: this is the slot with the largest calibration-to-evaluation drop risk.

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
text:
14.2 Why this is not leakage
An out-of-band result of this kind is usually a leak, so it was checked structurally rather than argued away. Four things were verified in src/models/model_1.py:

Observed discharge never enters the design matrix. The regressors are precipitation, PET and exponentially-weighted antecedent-precipitation indices. The “AR” in ARX is autoregression in the API state, not on observed \(Q\) — so the model remains comparable with the conceptual slots, which is exactly what config/project.yaml -> ml_state_note requires.
The multiplicative bias factor \(c\) is frozen at fit time. It is computed once inside fit() from the fitting window and only read in simulate(). It is not recomputed from the window being predicted — which would have been a textbook leak, and would have manufactured \(\beta \approx 1\) on any period.
Column means and standard deviations are likewise frozen in _fitted and restored by load().
The lazy-fit fallback routes to the calibration window through the guarded loader, never to the window passed to simulate(). The leak-safe path is the default, not an option.

The evaluation window played no part in any of this: src/common/data.py raises PermissionError unless LR_AGENT=a16, and no test or model sets that variable.

title: Five candidate models for daily streamflow of the Leaf River
section: 14.3 What it does and does not imply
text:
14.3 What it does and does not imply
It does not yet falsify H1. Two reasons to withhold judgement until a16:

These are calibration-period and internal-validation numbers. H1 is stated on the evaluation metric window 1949-01-01…1951-09-30, which no agent except a16 may touch.
That window is the wettest stretch of the record — mean \(Q\) ratio 1.29 versus calibration, runoff ratio 0.41 against 0.35 (a02). A regression carries no mass balance and no storage ceiling, so it has more room to degrade under a wetness shift than a conceptual model does. The conceptual slots also arrive at a16 calibrated, whereas the numbers above are mostly defaults.

What it does imply is that the interesting question has moved. The study was designed to measure how much complexity buys; it may instead measure how little. If slot 1 holds its ground on the evaluation window, the honest headline is that on a humid, energy-limited, snow-free basin with 40 years of clean forcing, a well-posed linear model in transformed space is competitive with conceptual hydrology — and H1, as pre-registered, is falsified in its first clause.
a16 must report that outcome plainly if it occurs, including the possibility that NSE(slot 1) > NSE(slot 4). A pre-registered hypothesis that fails is a result, not an error.

15.1 Builders a05–a09

Subclass src.common.model_api.BaseModel; set model_id to the slot id and kind exactly as in config/models.yaml. simulate() returns a pd.Series of mm/day on the full input index (warm-up included), deterministic given parameters and seed.
Read parameter bounds/defaults from config/models.yaml, do not hard-code them; expose them through param_specs() as ParamSpec objects (log_scale=True where the YAML says so).
Load data only via src.common.data; never call slice_run(..., "evaluation").
Ship the mass-balance test of your section as a pytest case in tests/test_model_N.py, plus

a determinism test (two identical calls give bitwise-identical output), (ii) a bounds test (defaults() inside bounds()), (iii) a 200-day dry-spell recession test against the analytic solution where one exists.

Integer-valued parameters (integer: true in the YAML) must be rounded inside the model, so the optimizer can keep searching a continuous box.

title: Implementation and Calibration
text: The other reports cover design (what to model, how to score it, how to search) and the final result. This one covers the middle: five agents turning specifications into tested code, and the calibration that followed. It exists because that step is where a study of this kind usually breaks — silently, through a leak or an unverified assumption — and because the record of how the numbers were produced is part of the result.
crumbs: Implementation and Calibration

title: Implementation and Calibration
section: 2.1 Three rules every builder had to follow
text:
2.1 Three rules every builder had to follow
These came from a03 and exist to keep the five models comparable and the held-out window clean.

Initial states must be parameter-derived, never observation-derived. The evaluation window offers only 92 warm-up days, so a model that needs observed flow to initialise cannot be evaluated fairly.
Integer and ordering constraints are enforced inside the model, so every optimizer sees a plain rectangular box. HBV’s K0 ≥ K1 ≥ K2 and SAC-SMA’s integer NINC are handled internally.
Scaling constants are frozen at calibration-window values, stored in the model artefact and restored by load() — never recomputed at prediction time.

Rule 3 is the one that matters most. Recomputing a mean or standard deviation at prediction time would quietly leak information from the window being predicted, and would do so without any obvious symptom.
crumbs: Implementation and Calibration

title: Implementation and Calibration
text:
2.2 How the implementations were verified
Because a wrong-but-plausible hydrological model produces perfectly reasonable-looking hydrographs, each builder had to prove correctness rather than demonstrate it:

Dual implementation. Every conceptual model has a numba-compiled kernel and a pure-Python reference path. All three pairs agree bitwise (max |difference| exactly 0.0 mm/day).
Mass balance. Closure was asserted over the full record and across random parameter sets: GR4J 4.0 × 10⁻¹¹ mm, HBV 9.9 × 10⁻¹² mm, SAC-SMA 1.4 × 10⁻¹¹ mm over 13,515 days.
Behavioural leak tests. Rather than inspecting code for leaks, builders poisoned the observed-flow column with nonsense and then deleted it, asserting the simulation was unchanged. Slot 5 went further and made leakage structurally impossible: its scaling object is a frozen dataclass with no fit method, and a source-scanning test asserts that no function on the prediction path contains a .mean() or .std() call at all.
Independent agreement. Slot 2’s implementation reproduced a03’s separately written prototype to four decimal places — two independent readings of the same specification landing on the same numbers.

title: Implementation and Calibration
section: 2.4 A specification conflict, and how it was resolved
text:
2.4 A specification conflict, and how it was resolved
SAC-SMA’s slowest store has a time constant of about 250 days, so its specification asked for 730 warm-up days. Only 366 exist in calibration, and 92 in evaluation. Extending backwards was impossible — earlier rows are the evaluation period.
The resolution, chosen by the user, was to cycle the available warm-up window repeatedly until the state variables reach a fixed point, then begin the real run from there. Only precipitation and PET are replayed, never observed flow, so the procedure is equally legal on the 92-day evaluation warm-up.
The proof that this removes the problem is not the convergence itself but its independence from the starting point: seeded from completely empty stores and from completely full stores, the converged state agrees to 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ relative. Convergence takes a median of 8 cycles (maximum 44 across 300 random parameter sets, against a cap of 200), and costs 16 % more runtime.
It is worth recording that the spin-up did not improve the score (objective 0.5678 with, 0.5680 without, at default parameters). It removes an arbitrary dependence on initial conditions, which is a correctness result, not a performance one.
crumbs: Implementation and Calibration

title: Implementation and Calibration
section: 3.1 The calibration ranking is not the out-of-sample ranking
text:
3.1 The calibration ranking is not the out-of-sample ranking
On the calibration window the order is the textbook complexity gradient: SAC-SMA > HBV > GR4J > regression. On the internal-validation window (1981-10-01…1988-09-30, never used for fitting) it changes: the regression moves from last to second.
More strikingly, the regression is the only model with a negative generalisation gap — it scores better on data it was not fitted to (−0.0178) while the three conceptual models each lose 0.037–0.042. That is the signature of a model that is not exploiting calibration-period idiosyncrasies, and it was the first concrete warning that the study’s central hypothesis was in trouble (see the H1-risk section of the model report).
crumbs: Implementation and Calibration

title: Implementation and Calibration
section: 3.2 Seed spread measures how hard each search is
text:
3.2 Seed spread measures how hard each search is
Running ten seeds was not ceremony. The spread across seeds differs by orders of magnitude between models:

GR4J (4 parameters): all ten seeds converged to identical parameters, standard deviation 0.00000. SCE-UA finds the global optimum on this surface every time.
SAC-SMA (15 parameters): standard deviation 0.0161, range 0.8835–0.9258. The surface is genuinely multimodal, and a single-seed calibration had a real chance of reporting a model 0.04 objective units worse than the one that was found.

Reassuringly, SAC-SMA’s best result (KGE 0.9500 / NSE 0.9017, via SCE-UA) reproduces an independent differential-evolution run by its builder (0.9500 / 0.9019) to four decimals — two different algorithms arriving at the same optimum.
crumbs: Implementation and Calibration

title: Implementation and Calibration
section: 3.3 Slot 5 was calibrated under a hard budget, and why
text:
3.3 Slot 5 was calibrated under a hard budget, and why
The LSTM is the only genuinely compute-constrained slot, and it is where the calibration phase failed first.
config/optimization.yaml declared a 90-minute cap on the hyperparameter search (study_timeout_s: 5400), a 60-epoch limit per trial, and a pruner. None of it was read by the code — the string outer never appears in the runner, and study.optimize() was called with no timeout= argument. The search ran for more than seven hours and produced no artefact at all (ISSUE-006).
It was replaced by a budgeted alternative agent (a15b-optimizer-5-fast) that enforces its deadline in its own code: a monotonic clock checked before every trial and inside the epoch loop. The same wrapper feeds Optuna’s pruner, so trials that are going nowhere are stopped early.

It finished in 7.6 minutes — 30 % of its cap — and produced the best calibration-side scores in the study. The result is nonetheless reported as a lower bound, for a reason its own agent identified: the selected hyperparameters are bound-active at hidden_size = 80, which is the reduced search’s own ceiling rather than the model’s. A fuller search should look above it.






ImportantThe transferable lesson



A budget that lives only in a configuration file is not a budget. The declared 90-minute cap and the enforced 25-minute cap differed by a factor of 3.6 on paper and by a factor of 55 in practice — seven hours against 7.6 minutes — because only one of them was written in code that runs.

text:
2.2 Metrics
Only two metrics are reported, both taken verbatim from src/common/metrics.py (Gupta et al. 2009; Nash and Sutcliffe 1970):
\[\mathrm{KGE} = 1 - \sqrt{(r-1)^2 + (\alpha-1)^2 + (\beta-1)^2},\qquad
\alpha = \frac{\sigma_s}{\sigma_o},\quad \beta = \frac{\mu_s}{\mu_o}\]
\[\mathrm{NSE} = 1 - \frac{\sum_t (s_t-o_t)^2}{\sum_t (o_t-\bar o)^2}\]
config/project.yaml → evaluation_protocol.final_report_metrics_only: true, so KGE and NSE are the only performance metrics in this report. The KGE components \(r\), \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) appear once, in Section 5, because hypothesis H5 is stated in terms of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) and cannot be adjudicated without them; they are not used to rank anything. Likewise the sub-period and log-space figures in H2/H3 are the pre-registered test statistics of those hypotheses, not performance claims.

title: Final evaluation on the held-out window: five calibrated models, five pre-declared ensembles, one winner
text:
2.3 Uncertainty
95 % confidence intervals come from a moving-block bootstrap (Künsch 1989; Politis and Romano 1994; Efron and Tibshirani 1994): 30-day blocks, 2,000 resamples, numpy.random.default_rng(42), block starts drawn uniformly from the 1,003-day metric window and concatenated to length 1,003. The same 2,000 index matrices are applied to every candidate, so differences between models are paired and their bootstrap distribution is a legitimate significance statement about the ranking. A 30-day block comfortably exceeds the basin’s 9–11 day recession time scale (a01/a02), so within-block serial correlation is preserved.

This table carries the most important diagnostic in the whole evaluation. The ranking is not stable across the three sub-periods, and the instability is concentrated in the first one.

In block 1 (Jan–Sep 1949, the wettest 273 days of the entire 40-year record and the block closest to the 92-day warm-up) the LSTM collapses to KGE 0.477 while the ridge regression reaches KGE 0.913 — the best of any candidate there.
In block 3 (WY1951, the driest of the three) the order reverses completely: the LSTM is the best candidate at KGE 0.957 / NSE 0.942, and the ridge is the worst at KGE 0.800.

Two mechanisms are consistent with this. (i) State initialisation. Slot 5 was calibrated with seq_len = 180 d and is started from \(h_0 = c_0 = 0\) on 1948-10-01, so the first ~180 days of the metric window are produced by a network whose recurrent state has not yet filled; the conceptual slots have the same problem in milder form (SAC-SMA’s spin-up removes its seed dependence but not the shortness of the window). (ii) Wetness extrapolation. Block 1 is 1.92× wetter than the calibration mean. A model with no mass balance and a short memory (the ridge, \(\lambda_{slow} = 0.97 \Rightarrow \tau \approx 33\) d) has little state to get wrong; a 180-day-memory network has a great deal.
This is reported as a diagnostic, not as a re-ranking. The protocol fixes the metric window at 1,003 days and the reported numbers are the 1,003-day numbers.

tab = pd.DataFrame({"model": [LABEL[SLOT_ID[s]] for s in range(1, 6)],
                    "α = σ_s/σ_o": [h["alpha"][str(s)] for s in range(1, 6)],

Markdown(f"""
**H5 is falsified.** The α clause holds for {n_a} of 5 models (SAC-SMA {f(h['alpha']['4'],3)} and the
LSTM {f(h['alpha']['5'],3)} exceed 1). The β clause holds for **{n_b} of 5**: *every* model
over-predicts the volume of the evaluation window, from GR4J's {f(h['beta']['2'],3)} to the LSTM's
{f(h['beta']['5'],3)}.

The sign is the opposite of what a01 and a04 expected. a04 had *measured* the transfer direction on
calibration-internal splits — moving a calibrated model to a wetter block lowered β by 0.068 on average —
and predicted β slightly below 1 here. The wetter evaluation window instead produced β **above** 1 for
all five. The mechanism is visible in @fig-resid and @fig-cumul: the surplus is not at the peaks (which
are all under-predicted, @fig-events) but in the recessions and the 1949 baseflow, i.e. the models drain
their stores too slowly when the antecedent wetness is far above anything in the calibration record.

H5 comes with its own rider: *"if a model shows β > 1.05 it is compensating a structural ET error."*
By that rider, {n_b105} of the 5 models — HBV-light, SAC-SMA and the LSTM — are flagged. Note that these
are exactly the three models with the largest KGE degradation (@sec-h4), and that GR4J, whose β is
{f(h['beta']['2'],4)}, is the model whose exchange parameter x2 explicitly removes water from the basin
(@sec-h8). The pre-registered rider and the pre-registered H8 point at the same place from two sides.

""")

Falsifiable statement: KGE(ens_physics_plus_ml) > KGE(ens_mean_conceptual).
Measured: 0.8890 vs 0.9058 — the conceptual-only mean is higher by 0.0167. H7 is falsified.
On NSE the comparison goes the other way (0.8790 vs 0.8638), which is worth stating because it shows where the ML member helps: adding the LSTM raises the squared-error skill and lowers the KGE, because it imports the LSTM’s volume bias (β 1.180) into the average. The hypothesis was pre-registered on KGE, and on KGE it fails. With the paired bootstrap, P(ens_mean_conceptual > ens_physics_plus_ml in KGE) is well inside the noise, so the falsification is of the point prediction, not a demonstration that family diversity is harmful.

6.1 Complexity versus performance


Code
s = met.loc[[SLOT_ID[i] for i in range(1, 6)]]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
for a, k in zip(ax, ["KGE", "NSE"]):
    a.semilogx(s["n_fitted"], s[k], "o", ms=9, color="#1f77b4")
    for i, r in s.iterrows():
        a.annotate(LABEL[i].split(" · ")[1], (r["n_fitted"], r[k]), fontsize=7,
                   xytext=(4, 5), textcoords="offset points")
    a.axhline(met.loc["bench_persistence_1day", k], ls=":", color="crimson", lw=1)
    a.set_xlabel("fitted quantities (parameters / coefficients / weights)"); a.set_ylabel(k)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()








Figure 11: Evaluation KGE and NSE against the number of fitted quantities (log axis). The dotted line is the one-day-persistence benchmark. Neither metric increases with complexity.





The complexity gradient a03 designed — 4 → 9 → 15 → 26 → 30,801 fitted quantities — produces no monotone gain in KGE on the held-out window, and its apparent positive association with NSE (Section 5.1) is carried by one model, the ridge, whose place in the gradient was supposed to be the floor. The 4-parameter GR4J has the highest single-model KGE; the 26-quantity regression has the highest NSE of anything in the study; the 30,801-weight-per-member LSTM is last on KGE. The calibration window told the opposite story (objective 0.865 → 0.885 → 0.919 → 0.926 → 0.938, monotone in complexity), and the internal-validation window already hinted at the reversal by promoting the ridge above GR4J and HBV-light.
The generalisable statement is not “simple models are better”. It is that on a humid, energy-limited, snow-free, unregulated basin with 40 years of clean lumped forcing, the marginal information content of additional model structure is small, and it is dominated by the mismatch between the calibration climate and the application climate. a04 quantified that mismatch cost in advance (0.02–0.06 objective units of regret between objective functions alone); the model-structure differences measured here, 0.004–0.03 KGE among the top seven, are of the same order or smaller.

6.2 High and low flows, and the wetter window


Code
M = sims[sims.in_metric_window]
o = M["Q_obs"].to_numpy()
qs = np.quantile(o, [0, .2, .4, .6, .8, 1.0])
labels = [f"Q{i*20}-{(i+1)*20}%" for i in range(5)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
w = 0.15
for j, s_ in enumerate(range(1, 6)):
    v = []
    for i in range(5):
        m = (o >= qs[i]) & (o <= qs[i + 1])
        v.append((M[f"model_{s_}"].to_numpy()[m] - o[m]).mean())
    ax.bar(np.arange(5) + (j - 2) * w, v, width=w, label=LABEL[SLOT_ID[s_]])
ax.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.8); ax.set_ylabel("mean error (mm/d)")
ax.set_xticks(range(5)); ax.set_xticklabels(labels); ax.legend(fontsize=7)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()








Figure 12: Volume error by flow stratum: the mean of (simulated - observed) inside observed-flow quintiles of the metric window. Positive = over-prediction. This is a diagnostic, not a reported metric.





The evaluation window is the wettest stretch of the record (a02: mean-Q ratio 1.29, runoff ratio 0.407 against 0.35 on calibration) but its maximum flow, 45.9 mm/d, is below the calibration maximum 64.0 mm/d — there is no magnitude extrapolation, only a wetness shift. The models’ response to that shift is consistent and unflattering: they over-predict the low and middle strata and under-predict the top stratum, which is precisely the pattern that produces β > 1 (H5) together with the systematic under-prediction of the January 1950 peak (Figure 3: all five models miss the 45.9 mm/d peak, by 9–21 mm/d).
Which models extrapolate better? By the KGE degradation in Section 5.4, the order is GR4J (0.020) ≈ ARX ridge (0.020) < HBV-light (0.062) < SAC-SMA (0.075) < LSTM (0.129) — i.e. inversely ordered by the amount of state and the number of fitted quantities, with the single exception that the ridge (26 quantities) transfers as well as the 4-parameter GR4J and actually gains on NSE. Models with long-memory stores and many degrees of freedom carry their calibration climate with them.

text:
6.3 Failure modes

LSTM, first 180 days. KGE 0.477 in block 1 against 0.957 in block 3 (Table 7). Zero-initialised recurrent state plus a 180-day lookback plus the wettest year of the record. This is the largest single failure in the study, and it is a protocol-interaction failure — 92 warm-up days are not enough for a 180-day-memory model — not necessarily a failure of the architecture.
Seed dependence of the LSTM. 0.060 KGE standard deviation across three seeds, versus a total top-seven spread of 0.038. a15b’s own handoff flagged that its seed spread (0.0069 on internal validation) was 69× a10’s convergence tolerance; on the evaluation window the spread is an order of magnitude larger again.
Peak under-prediction, all models. Every model misses the 1950-01-08 event (Figure 3). SAC-SMA is the least bad on the 20 largest days (NSE 0.506).
Fitted ensemble weights. See H6: NNLS weights fitted on 2,557 held-out calibration days still transferred worse than equal weights.
No candidate produced a NaN or a negative flow, and the minimum simulated flow over all ten candidates is 0.0222 mm/d, comfortably positive on a perennial river.

Different metric. The prior study reports \(KGE_{ss}\), the Knoben et al. (2019) benchmarked skill score $ (KGE + 0.4142)/ $, not KGE itself. Converted, its best out-of-sample figure \(KGE_{ss} = 0.856\) is KGE 0.796 and its baseline model’s testing figure \(KGE_{ss} = 0.803\) is KGE 0.721. The prior study does prescribe exactly this 1948-10-01…1951-09-30 run with a Oct–Dec 1948 warm-up (FinalReport.qmd § 5.4.5) — that is where this project’s period definition comes from — but it uses that window for model development and demonstration, not as its held-out test set.

The prior study initialises its lower-zone state from the observed flow on the first day of the window, \(XX_2(0) \approx QQ^{obs}(1)/\theta K_{2Q}\) (FinalReport.qmd § 5.4.4). Every model in this project uses parameter-derived initial states and never reads an observation inside the evaluation window (a03 decision 3). section: 8.1 The leakage concern that cannot be fully ruled out
text:
8.1 The leakage concern that cannot be fully ruled out
One: the evaluation window was chosen by the user, in advance, from a prior study that had already looked at it. config/project.yaml → periods takes its definition verbatim from the 2025 report (Section 6.5), which ran, plotted and discussed exactly these 1,095 days. No parameter of any model in this project was fitted on those days — that is verifiable and was verified — but the period itself is not a blind draw, and the project’s model portfolio (a03) was designed by agents who had read a02’s description of that period’s wetness. a02 was explicitly permitted to describe the whole record, and it did: “the evaluation window is the wettest part of the record, mean Q ratio 1.29” appears in context/CONTEXT.md and was available to every builder. That is a soft, unquantifiable influence on model choice, and it cannot be undone after the fact. It should be assumed to bias the results optimistically by an unknown, probably small, amount.
Two smaller ones, both recorded rather than resolved: (i) slot 5’s hyperparameters, early stopping and seed ensemble were all selected on the calibration internal-validation window, so its calibration numbers are optimistically biased (a09’s own open issue) and the H4 degradation is correspondingly inflated — though the verdict survives any plausible correction, since its drop exceeds the next largest by 0.041 NSE; (ii) the NNLS weights were fitted on calibration data but on the same window that a11–a15 used for model selection, so ens_nnls_calibration inherits that window’s selection bias — which is part of why it under-performs here (H6b).
